outcomes: Learner can locate magnetic poles and show that like poles repel and unlike attract
prompt: Draw two bar magnets for each case and add arrows showing push or pull: (a) N facing S, (b) S facing S.
prompt_hi: Har case ke liye do bar magnet banao aur teer se dikhao kheenchna ya dhakelna: (a) N ke saamne S, (b) S ke saamne S.
answer: (a) Arrows pointing towards each other: attraction. (b) Arrows pointing away from each other: repulsion.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can locate magnetic poles and show that like poles repel and unlike attract
prompt: Golu says: 'If I cut my magnet in half, I'll get a north-only magnet and a south-only magnet.' What is wrong?
prompt_hi: Golu kehta hai: 'Agar main magnet ko beech se kaat doon, toh ek sirf-north aur ek sirf-south magnet milega.' Galti kya hai?
answer: Each piece has both a north and a south pole; magnetic poles always come in pairs.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can locate magnetic poles and show that like poles repel and unlike attract
prompt: Teach your friend the 'rules' of magnets: poles, attraction and repulsion, and how to look after magnets.
prompt_hi: Apne dost ko magnet ke 'niyam' sikhao: poles, kheenchna aur dhakelna, aur magnet ki dekhbhaal kaise karein.
answer: Key ideas: every magnet has N and S poles, strongest at the ends; like poles repel, unlike attract; repulsion is the sure test; breaking a magnet makes new poles; strength isn't size; heating, hammering or dropping weakens magnets, so store them in pairs with keepers.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can locate magnetic poles and show that like poles repel and unlike attract
prompt: From last time: what is the sure test to know that an object is a magnet?
prompt_hi: Pichhli baar se: kisi cheez ke magnet hone ka pakka test kya hai?
answer: Repulsion: if it pushes away a pole of a known magnet, it is a magnet.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can use a freely suspended magnet or compass to find directions
prompt: A bar magnet hangs freely from a thread. When it stops moving, in which directions do its ends point?
prompt_hi: Ek bar magnet dhaage se khula latka hai. Jab woh rukta hai, toh uske sire kis disha mein hote hain?
answer: North and south (roughly); its north pole points north.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can use a freely suspended magnet or compass to find directions
prompt: Your compass needle has settled. How do you find east?
prompt_hi: Tumhare compass ki suyi ruk gayi hai. East (poorab) kaise pata karoge?
answer: Turn the compass so the N on the dial lines up with the needle's north end; east is then marked E, a quarter turn clockwise from north (to your right if you face north).

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can use a freely suspended magnet or compass to find directions
prompt: Predict: you hang a bar magnet from a thread, gently turn it to point east-west, and let go. What will happen?
prompt_hi: Guess karo: bar magnet ko dhaage se latka ke halke se east-west mein ghumaao aur chhod do. Kya hoga?
answer: It swings and settles back into the north-south direction.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can use a freely suspended magnet or compass to find directions
prompt: Predict: you stroke a straightened steel paper clip about 30 times in one direction with one pole of a magnet, then float it on a piece of cork in a bowl of water. What will the clip do?
prompt_hi: Guess karo: seedhi ki hui steel ki paper clip ko magnet ke ek pole se ek hi disha mein 30 baar ragdo, phir use cork ke tukde pe rakh ke paani ki katori mein tairao. Clip kya karegi?
answer: It turns and settles pointing north-south like a compass, because stroking made it a magnet.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can use a freely suspended magnet or compass to find directions
prompt: Predict: you slowly bring a bar magnet close to a compass lying on the table. What happens to the needle?
prompt_hi: Guess karo: mez pe rakhe compass ke paas dheere-dheere bar magnet laao. Suyi ka kya hoga?
answer: The needle swings away from north and turns towards the magnet (its north end is pulled by the magnet's south pole and pushed by its north pole); magnets disturb a compass.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can use a freely suspended magnet or compass to find directions
prompt: You said the floating paper clip points north-south. Why does it do that?
prompt_hi: Tumne kaha tairti hui paper clip uttar-dakshin mein rukti hai. Woh aisa kyon karti hai?
answer: Stroking turned it into a magnet, and since the Earth behaves like a giant magnet, the clip magnet lines up north-south.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can use a freely suspended magnet or compass to find directions
prompt: Compare a compass placed on a wooden table and one placed on top of a steel almirah. Which reading can you trust, and why?
prompt_hi: Lakdi ki mez pe rakha compass aur steel ki almari ke upar rakha compass compare karo. Kis reading pe bharosa kar sakte ho, aur kyon?
answer: The one on the wooden table; the iron or steel in the almirah can pull on the needle and give a wrong reading.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can use a freely suspended magnet or compass to find directions
prompt: Your group must find which wall of a new classroom faces east, using a compass. What steps will you follow?
prompt_hi: Tumhare group ko compass se pata karna hai ki nayi class ki kaunsi deewar east ki taraf hai. Kaun se steps loge?
answer: Hold the compass flat, away from iron and magnets; let the needle settle; turn the compass so N lines up with the needle's north end; look in the direction marked E; the wall in that direction faces east.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can use a freely suspended magnet or compass to find directions
prompt: Long ago, sailors far out at sea, with clouds hiding the Sun and the stars, still found their direction. How?
prompt_hi: Bahut pehle naavik samundar ke beech mein, jab baadal Suraj aur taaron ko chhupa dete the, tab bhi disha dhundh lete the. Kaise?
answer: They used a magnetic compass (a magnetised needle or lodestone), which points north-south in any weather.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can use a freely suspended magnet or compass to find directions
prompt: Draw a compass face and mark N, E, S and W. If you face north, which direction is on your right?
prompt_hi: Compass ka chehra banao aur N, E, S, W likho. Agar tum north ki taraf mooh karo, toh tumhare right haath pe kaunsi disha hogi?
answer: East is on your right, west on your left and south behind you.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can use a freely suspended magnet or compass to find directions
prompt: Golu says: 'A compass needle points north because it is so cold at the North Pole, and magnets like cold.' What is wrong?
prompt_hi: Golu kehta hai: 'Compass ki suyi north isliye dikhati hai kyonki North Pole pe bahut thand hai, aur magnet ko thand pasand hai.' Galti kya hai?
answer: Cold has nothing to do with it; the Earth behaves like a giant magnet, and the needle lines up with it.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can use a freely suspended magnet or compass to find directions
prompt: Explain to a younger child how to make a pin-and-water compass (with an adult holding the pin) and why it works.
prompt_hi: Ek chhote bachche ko samjhao ki pin aur paani wala compass kaise banate hain (pin kisi bade se pakadwa ke) aur woh kaam kyon karta hai.
answer: Key ideas: stroke a steel pin or straightened paper clip many times in one direction with one pole of a magnet (an adult helps with anything sharp); float it on cork or a leaf in water; it turns north-south because it became a magnet and lines up with the Earth's magnetism; keep it away from other magnets and iron.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can use a freely suspended magnet or compass to find directions
prompt: From last time: the end of a freely hanging magnet that points north is called its ___ pole.
prompt_hi: Pichhli baar se: khule latke magnet ka jo sira north ki taraf hota hai, use ___ pole kehte hain.
answer: North (north-seeking) pole.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can measure lengths with a scale correctly (zero error, eye position) and use SI units
prompt: How many centimetres are in 1 metre, and how many millimetres are in 1 centimetre?
prompt_hi: 1 metre mein kitne centimetre hote hain, aur 1 centimetre mein kitne millimetre?
answer: 100 cm in 1 m; 10 mm in 1 cm.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can measure lengths with a scale correctly (zero error, eye position) and use SI units
prompt: One end of a pencil is at 0 cm and the other end at 14.5 cm. How long is the pencil?
prompt_hi: Pencil ka ek sira 0 cm pe hai aur doosra 14.5 cm pe. Pencil kitni lambi hai?

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can measure lengths with a scale correctly (zero error, eye position) and use SI units
prompt: Predict: you and your father both measure the length of the dining table in handspans. Will you get the same number? Why?
prompt_hi: Guess karo: tum aur papa dono khaane ki mez ki lambai baalisht se naapte ho. Kya dono ka number same aayega? Kyon?
answer: No; you will get a bigger number because your handspan is shorter. Body measures differ between people.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can measure lengths with a scale correctly (zero error, eye position) and use SI units
prompt: Your scale's end is broken, so the first clear mark is 1 cm. An eraser lined up from 1 cm ends at 5.5 cm. Predict what Golu, who only reads the end mark, will say, and what the real length is.
prompt_hi: Tumhari scale ka sira toota hai, pehla saaf nishaan 1 cm hai. 1 cm se rakha rubber 5.5 cm pe khatam hota hai. Guess karo, jo Golu sirf aakhri nishaan padhta hai, woh kya bolega, aur asli lambai kya hai?
answer: Golu will say 5.5 cm; the real length is 5.5 − 1 = 4.5 cm.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can measure lengths with a scale correctly (zero error, eye position) and use SI units
prompt: Predict: Riya reads the same mark on a scale once from the left, once from directly above and once from the right. Will all three readings be the same?
prompt_hi: Guess karo: Riya scale ka ek hi nishaan ek baar left se, ek baar seedha upar se aur ek baar right se padhti hai. Kya teeno reading same aayengi?
answer: No; readings taken from the sides will be off, and only the reading from directly above is correct.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can measure lengths with a scale correctly (zero error, eye position) and use SI units
prompt: Why can't a tailor note your kurta measurements in her handspans?
prompt_hi: Darzi aapke kurte ka naap apni baalisht mein kyon nahi likh sakti?
answer: Handspans differ between people, so anyone else cutting the cloth would get different sizes; a standard unit like cm on a measuring tape gives the same value for everyone.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can measure lengths with a scale correctly (zero error, eye position) and use SI units
prompt: Two ways of measuring a book: (A) the scale laid along the book's edge starting at 0; (B) the scale held at a slant, starting from its outer edge. Which is correct, and what is wrong with the other?
prompt_hi: Kitaab naapne ke do tareeke: (A) scale kitaab ke kinare ke saath, 0 se shuru; (B) scale tircha, uske bahari kinare se shuru. Kaunsa sahi hai, aur doosre mein kya galat hai?
answer: A is correct. B is slanted, not along the length, and starts from the edge instead of the zero mark, so it gives a wrong reading.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can measure lengths with a scale correctly (zero error, eye position) and use SI units
prompt: The distance between the two sets of stumps on a cricket pitch is about 20 m. How many centimetres is 20 m?
prompt_hi: Cricket pitch pe dono wicket ke beech ki doori lagbhag 20 m hai. 20 m kitne centimetre hue?

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can measure lengths with a scale correctly (zero error, eye position) and use SI units
prompt: Your school is 2 km from home. Each of your steps is about 50 cm long. Roughly how many steps is it?
prompt_hi: Tumhara school ghar se 2 km door hai. Tumhara ek kadam lagbhag 50 cm ka hai. Lagbhag kitne kadam hue?

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can measure lengths with a scale correctly (zero error, eye position) and use SI units
prompt: A ruler picture shows a leaf that starts at the 2 cm mark, and its tip is 3 small divisions after the 9 cm mark. Write the leaf's length in cm and in mm.
prompt_hi: Scale ki ek picture mein patti 2 cm ke nishaan se shuru hoti hai aur uski nok 9 cm ke baad 3 chhote khaane aage hai. Patti ki lambai cm aur mm mein likho.
answer: The tip is at 9.3 cm; length = 9.3 − 2 = 7.3 cm = 73 mm.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can measure lengths with a scale correctly (zero error, eye position) and use SI units
prompt: Golu says: 'Our door is 2 metres tall, which is 2 feet.' What is wrong?
prompt_hi: Golu kehta hai: 'Hamara darwaza 2 metre ooncha hai, yaani 2 foot.' Galti kya hai?
answer: A metre is not a foot: 1 m is about 3.3 feet (1 foot is about 30 cm), so 2 m is about 6.6 feet.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can measure lengths with a scale correctly (zero error, eye position) and use SI units
prompt: Teach your younger sister three rules for measuring a pencil correctly with a scale.
prompt_hi: Apni chhoti behen ko scale se pencil sahi naapne ke teen niyam sikhao.
answer: Key ideas: lay the scale along the pencil, touching it; start from the zero mark, or another full mark and subtract; keep your eye directly above the reading; write the number with its unit.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can measure lengths with a scale correctly (zero error, eye position) and use SI units
prompt: From last time: what is the SI unit of length?
prompt_hi: Pichhli baar se: lambai ki SI unit kya hai?
answer: The metre (m).

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can measure curved lengths with a thread
prompt: List the steps to measure a curved line in your notebook using a thread.
prompt_hi: Notebook mein bani tedhi line ko dhaage se naapne ke steps batao.
answer: Place the thread at the start and lay it carefully along the curve; mark where the curve ends; straighten the thread; measure the marked length on a scale.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can measure curved lengths with a thread
prompt: What can you use to measure around your head or around a round bottle?
prompt_hi: Apne sir ke chaaron taraf ya gol botal ke chaaron taraf naapne ke liye kya use kar sakte ho?
answer: A flexible measuring tape (tailor's tape), or a thread that you then measure with a scale.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can measure curved lengths with a thread
prompt: A curved line's two ends are 8 cm apart in a straight line. Predict: will a thread laid along the curve measure less than, equal to, or more than 8 cm?
prompt_hi: Ek tedhi line ke dono sire seedhe 8 cm door hain. Guess karo: line ke saath bichhaya dhaaga 8 cm se kam, barabar ya zyada naapega?
answer: More than 8 cm; a curve between two points is longer than the straight line joining them.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can measure curved lengths with a thread
prompt: Predict: Golu measures the same curve with a rubber band instead of a thread, stretching it a bit to fit. Will his answer be correct?
prompt_hi: Guess karo: Golu wahi tedhi line dhaage ki jagah rubber band se naapta hai, thoda kheench ke. Kya uska answer sahi hoga?
answer: No; a rubber band stretches and shrinks back, so its length changes and the reading is unreliable (usually too short once it relaxes).

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can measure curved lengths with a thread
prompt: Predict: you measure around a cricket ball with a thread. Which is closest: 7 cm, 23 cm or 50 cm?
prompt_hi: Guess karo: cricket ball ke chaaron taraf dhaage se naapo. Sabse kareeb kya hoga: 7 cm, 23 cm ya 50 cm?
answer: About 23 cm (a cricket ball's circumference is about 22-23 cm).

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can measure curved lengths with a thread
prompt: You got 12 cm with the thread for a curve whose ends were 8 cm apart. Why is it longer?
prompt_hi: Jis tedhi line ke sire 8 cm door the, dhaage se tumhe 12 cm mila. Ye lamba kyon hai?
answer: The curve bends, so the path along it from start to end is longer than the straight path between the ends.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can measure curved lengths with a thread
prompt: On a map, the straight line from town A to town B is 5 cm, and the winding road measured with a thread is 7 cm. The scale is 1 cm = 10 km. What are the two distances, and which one would a bus travel?
prompt_hi: Map pe shehar A se B tak seedhi line 5 cm hai, aur ghoomti sadak dhaage se 7 cm. Scale hai 1 cm = 10 km. Dono dooriyan kitni hain, aur inme se kaunsi doori bus tay karegi?
answer: Straight-line distance 50 km; road distance 70 km. The bus travels 70 km along the road.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can measure curved lengths with a thread
prompt: How would you measure the thickness around (the girth of) a neem tree trunk?
prompt_hi: Neem ke ped ke tane ki motai, yaani uske chaaron taraf ki lambai, kaise naapoge?
answer: Wrap a thread or flexible tape around the trunk at one height, mark where it meets itself, then measure that length with a scale or tape.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can measure curved lengths with a thread
prompt: On a school map, the Ganga's curved path between two cities measures 15 cm with a thread. The map scale is 1 cm = 20 km. How long is the river between the cities?
prompt_hi: School ke map pe do shehron ke beech Ganga ka tedha raasta dhaage se 15 cm aata hai. Map ka scale 1 cm = 20 km hai. Shehron ke beech nadi kitni lambi hai?

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can measure curved lengths with a thread
prompt: Draw a wavy line. Then draw two more pictures: the thread laid along it, and the same thread straightened beside a scale. What does each picture show?
prompt_hi: Ek lehriya line banao. Phir do aur picture banao: uske upar bichha dhaaga, aur wahi dhaaga scale ke paas seedha kiya hua. Har picture kya dikhati hai?
answer: Picture 1: the thread follows the curve, with the start and end marked. Picture 2: the straightened thread lies on the scale from 0 to the end mark; that reading is the curve's length.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can measure curved lengths with a thread
prompt: Riya wraps a thread around a bangle but leaves gaps where the thread doesn't touch the bangle. She gets 18 cm. What might be wrong?
prompt_hi: Riya chudi ke chaaron taraf dhaaga lapet-ti hai par kai jagah dhaaga chudi ko chhoota nahi, beech mein jagah reh jaati hai. Use 18 cm milta hai. Kya galat ho sakta hai?
answer: The thread did not follow the bangle closely; where it bulged away, it made a bigger loop, so 18 cm is probably too long. She should wrap it snugly with no gaps or overlaps.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can measure curved lengths with a thread
prompt: Explain to your friend how to find the real road distance between two towns on a map, step by step.
prompt_hi: Apne dost ko step by step samjhao ki map pe do shehron ke beech sadak ki asli doori kaise pata karein.
answer: Key ideas: lay a thread along the road on the map; mark the ends; straighten the thread and measure it in cm; multiply by the map scale (e.g. 1 cm = 10 km) to get the real distance.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can measure curved lengths with a thread
prompt: From last time: why do we straighten the thread before measuring it with a scale?
prompt_hi: Pichhli baar se: dhaage ko scale se naapne se pehle seedha kyon karte hain?
answer: A straight scale can only measure a straight length; the straightened thread's length is the same as the curve's length.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can describe motion as linear, circular or oscillatory using a reference point
prompt: Name the type of motion: (a) a train on a straight track, (b) a giant wheel turning, (c) a swing.
prompt_hi: Gati ka type batao: (a) seedhi patri pe train, (b) ghoomta hua giant wheel, (c) jhoola.
answer: (a) Linear, (b) circular, (c) oscillatory.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can describe motion as linear, circular or oscillatory using a reference point
prompt: What is a reference point? Give an example.
prompt_hi: Reference point kya hota hai? Ek example do.
answer: A fixed object or place we compare positions with to decide if something is moving, e.g. a tree beside the road, the platform or a signboard.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can describe motion as linear, circular or oscillatory using a reference point
prompt: Predict: Riya sits in a moving bus and her friend Aman stands at the bus stop. Will Aman say Riya is moving? Will the boy sitting next to Riya say she is moving?
prompt_hi: Guess karo: Riya chalti bus mein baithi hai aur Aman bus stop pe khada hai. Kya Aman kahega Riya chal rahi hai? Riya ke bagal wala ladka kya kahega?
answer: Aman says she is moving, because her position changes compared with the bus stop; the boy next to her says she is at rest, because her position doesn't change compared with him.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can describe motion as linear, circular or oscillatory using a reference point
prompt: Predict: you tie an eraser to a thread, hold the other end, pull the eraser to one side and let go. What kind of motion will you see?
prompt_hi: Guess karo: rubber ko dhaage se baandho, dhaage ka doosra sira pakdo, rubber ko ek taraf kheench ke chhod do. Kaisi gati dikhegi?
answer: Oscillatory motion: it swings to and fro about the middle position, like a pendulum.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can describe motion as linear, circular or oscillatory using a reference point
prompt: Predict: you sit in a train standing still at the platform, and the train on the next track starts moving. How might it feel, and how can you check which train is moving?
prompt_hi: Guess karo: tum platform pe khadi train mein baithe ho, aur bagal wali patri ki train chalne lagti hai. Kaisa lag sakta hai, aur kaise check karoge kaunsi train chal rahi hai?
answer: You may feel that your own train is moving; check by looking at a fixed reference point like the platform or a building.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can describe motion as linear, circular or oscillatory using a reference point
prompt: You said a swing is oscillatory, not circular. Why?
prompt_hi: Tumne kaha jhoola oscillatory hai, circular nahi. Kyon?
answer: It moves to and fro about a central rest position, repeating the same path, and never goes all the way round in a circle.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can describe motion as linear, circular or oscillatory using a reference point
prompt: Just by watching (never touch a moving fan or wheel), compare the motion of the tip of a ceiling fan blade with the motion of the centre (axle) of a rolling bicycle wheel.
prompt_hi: Sirf dekh ke (chalte pankhe ya pahiye ko kabhi mat chhoona), pankhe ki blade ki nok ki gati aur chalti cycle ke pahiye ke beech (dhure) ki gati compare karo.
answer: The fan blade tip moves in a circle while the fan stays in place (circular). The bicycle axle moves in a straight line along the road (linear), while the wheel also turns round it.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can describe motion as linear, circular or oscillatory using a reference point
prompt: Name the type of motion: a child going down a straight slide, the tip of a clock's hand, a plucked sitar string.
prompt_hi: Gati ka type batao: seedhi slide se neeche aata bachcha, ghadi ki suyi ki nok, chhedi hui sitar ki taar.
answer: Slide: linear. Clock-hand tip: circular. Sitar string: oscillatory (vibrating to and fro).

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can describe motion as linear, circular or oscillatory using a reference point
prompt: At a mela, describe the motion of (a) a boat ride that swings to and fro, (b) a merry-go-round, (c) a toy train going straight. Which ride shows two types of motion if its horses also move up and down?
prompt_hi: Mele mein in sab ki gati batao: (a) aage-peechhe jhoolti naav, (b) merry-go-round, (c) seedhi chalti toy train. Agar merry-go-round ke ghode upar-neeche bhi hote hain, toh kis ride mein do tarah ki gati hai?
answer: (a) Oscillatory, (b) circular, (c) linear. The merry-go-round: its horses go round (circular) and up and down (oscillatory) at the same time.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can describe motion as linear, circular or oscillatory using a reference point
prompt: Draw arrows to show the path of linear, circular and oscillatory motion. Describe each drawing in words.
prompt_hi: Linear, circular aur oscillatory gati ka raasta teer se banao. Har drawing ko shabdon mein batao.
answer: Linear: a straight arrow. Circular: an arrow going round a circle. Oscillatory: a two-headed arrow or short arc showing to and fro about a middle point.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can describe motion as linear, circular or oscillatory using a reference point
prompt: Golu says: 'A tree is never moving and a running dog is always moving. We don't need a reference point.' What is the problem?
prompt_hi: Golu kehta hai: 'Ped kabhi nahi chalta aur daudta kutta hamesha chalta hai. Reference point ki zaroorat nahi.' Dikkat kya hai?
answer: Whether something is moving depends on what we compare it with: seen from a moving bus, the tree seems to move backwards, and a dog running alongside the bus can stay level with a passenger. We always describe motion with respect to a reference point.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can describe motion as linear, circular or oscillatory using a reference point
prompt: Explain to your cousin the three types of motion using things in a park, and what a reference point is.
prompt_hi: Apne cousin ko park ki cheezon se teeno tarah ki gati samjhao, aur reference point kya hota hai.
answer: Key ideas: linear (a straight slide), circular (a merry-go-round), oscillatory (a swing); a reference point is a fixed object we compare position with, and whether something is moving depends on it.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can describe motion as linear, circular or oscillatory using a reference point
prompt: From last time: what type of motion does the pendulum of a wall clock show?
prompt_hi: Pichhli baar se: deewar ghadi ke pendulum ki gati kis type ki hai?
answer: Oscillatory motion.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can test properties like hardness, lustre, solubility, transparency and float-sink
prompt: Sort into transparent, translucent and opaque: clear glass, butter paper, a wooden board, clean water, a steel plate, frosted bathroom glass.
prompt_hi: Transparent, translucent aur opaque mein baanto: saaf kaanch, butter paper, lakdi ka phatta, saaf paani, steel ki plate, bathroom ka dhundhla kaanch.
answer: Transparent: clear glass, clean water. Translucent: butter paper, frosted glass. Opaque: wooden board, steel plate.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can test properties like hardness, lustre, solubility, transparency and float-sink
prompt: What is lustre? Name two materials that have it.
prompt_hi: Lustre kya hai? Do materials batao jinme ye hota hai.
answer: Lustre is the shine on a surface; metals such as copper, steel, gold, silver and aluminium have it, especially when freshly polished or cut.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can test properties like hardness, lustre, solubility, transparency and float-sink
prompt: Predict which of these will dissolve in water: salt, sand, sugar, chalk powder, a few drops of cooking oil.
prompt_hi: Guess karo inme se kya paani mein ghulega: namak, ret, cheeni, chalk ka powder, khaane ke tel ki kuch boondein.
answer: Salt and sugar dissolve; sand and chalk powder settle at the bottom; the oil floats as a separate layer and doesn't dissolve.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can test properties like hardness, lustre, solubility, transparency and float-sink
prompt: Predict which of these float and which sink in a bucket of water: a big wooden log, a small iron nail, a hollow plastic ball, a stone.
prompt_hi: Guess karo baalti ke paani mein kaun tairega aur kaun doobega: bada lakdi ka latha, chhoti lohe ki keel, khokhli plastic ki ball, ek patthar.
answer: The log and the plastic ball float; the nail and the stone sink.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can test properties like hardness, lustre, solubility, transparency and float-sink
prompt: Predict: you place an empty steel katori gently, right side up, on the water in a bucket. Will it float or sink? What if it fills with water?
prompt_hi: Guess karo: khaali steel ki katori ko seedha baalti ke paani pe halke se rakho. Tairegi ya doobegi? Aur agar usme paani bhar jaaye toh?
answer: The empty katori floats because of its hollow shape; if it fills with water it sinks. Shape matters, not just the material.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can test properties like hardness, lustre, solubility, transparency and float-sink
prompt: You said the heavy log floats but the light nail sinks. Why?
prompt_hi: Tumne kaha bhaari latha tairta hai aur halki keel doobti hai. Kyon?
answer: Floating depends on the material and shape, not on total weight: wood is light for its size compared with water, while iron is heavy for its size, so the nail sinks.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can test properties like hardness, lustre, solubility, transparency and float-sink
prompt: A clear plastic tumbler and a glass tumbler look the same. Name one property that differs and how you could test it safely.
prompt_hi: Plastic ka saaf tumbler aur kaanch ka tumbler ek jaise dikhte hain. Ek property batao jo alag hai aur use safely kaise test karoge.
answer: For example, flexibility: press gently and the plastic bends a little while the glass stays rigid; the glass would break if dropped, so don't test by dropping. Tapping also gives a different sound.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can test properties like hardness, lustre, solubility, transparency and float-sink
prompt: Why are bathroom windows often made of frosted glass instead of clear glass?
prompt_hi: Bathroom ki khidkiyan aksar saaf kaanch ki jagah dhundhle kaanch ki kyon hoti hain?
answer: Frosted glass is translucent: it lets light in, but people outside can't see in clearly, which gives privacy.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can test properties like hardness, lustre, solubility, transparency and float-sink
prompt: Fishing nets have floats tied along the top edge and weights along the bottom. What might the floats and weights be made of, and why?
prompt_hi: Machhli pakadne ke jaal mein upar ke kinare pe float aur neeche ke kinare pe vazan bandhe hote hain. Float aur vazan kis cheez ke ho sakte hain, aur kyon?
answer: Floats: materials that float, such as plastic, thermocol or wood. Weights: materials that sink, such as lead, iron or stones. Together they hold the net upright like a wall in the water.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can test properties like hardness, lustre, solubility, transparency and float-sink
prompt: Make a table with columns shiny?, hard?, dissolves?, floats? and fill it in for a steel spoon, a wooden spoon and a piece of wax.
prompt_hi: Ek table banao jisme columns hon: chamakdaar?, sakht?, ghulta hai?, tairta hai? aur steel ki chammach, lakdi ki chammach aur mom ke tukde ke liye bharo.
answer: Steel spoon: shiny ✓, hard ✓, dissolves ✗, floats ✗. Wooden spoon: shiny ✗, hard ✓, dissolves ✗, floats ✓. Wax: shiny ✗, hard ✗ (a fingernail scratches it), dissolves ✗, floats ✓.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can test properties like hardness, lustre, solubility, transparency and float-sink
prompt: Golu says: 'Sugar and white sand look the same, so both will dissolve in water.' What is wrong?
prompt_hi: Golu kehta hai: 'Cheeni aur safed ret ek jaise dikhte hain, isliye dono paani mein ghul jaayenge.' Galti kya hai?
answer: Looks don't tell us properties: sugar dissolves but sand doesn't, so we have to test.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can test properties like hardness, lustre, solubility, transparency and float-sink
prompt: Explain to a friend five properties we can test in materials, with one quick home test for each.
prompt_hi: Ek dost ko paanch properties samjhao jo hum materials mein test kar sakte hain, aur har ek ka ghar pe karne wala ek chhota test.
answer: Key ideas: lustre (look for shine); hardness (press or scratch gently with a fingernail); transparency (hold it up to a light); solubility (stir a little into water); floating or sinking (put it in a bucket of water).

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can test properties like hardness, lustre, solubility, transparency and float-sink
prompt: From last time: what do we call a material that lets some light through, but we can't see clearly through it?
prompt_hi: Pichhli baar se: jo material thodi roshni jaane deta hai par usme se saaf nahi dikhta, use kya kehte hain?
answer: Translucent.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can group materials by properties and relate properties to uses
prompt: Name the material each object is made of: a notebook, a lota, a raincoat, a window pane.
prompt_hi: Har object kis material se bana hai, batao: notebook, lota, raincoat, khidki ka sheesha.
answer: Notebook: paper. Lota: brass, copper or steel. Raincoat: plastic or another waterproof material. Window pane: glass.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can group materials by properties and relate properties to uses
prompt: Group these materials into transparent and opaque: glass, wood, clear plastic sheet, iron, cardboard.
prompt_hi: In materials ko transparent aur opaque mein baanto: kaanch, lakdi, saaf plastic sheet, loha, gatta.
answer: Transparent: glass, clear plastic sheet. Opaque: wood, iron, cardboard.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can group materials by properties and relate properties to uses
prompt: Predict (don't touch to check!): after cooking, which part of a frying pan will be hot, the metal pan or its plastic handle? Why?
prompt_hi: Guess karo (chhoo ke check mat karna!): khaana banane ke baad kadhai ka kaunsa hissa garam hoga, dhaatu wala ya plastic ka handle? Kyon?
answer: The metal pan is hot; the plastic handle stays fairly cool, because heat does not pass through plastic easily.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can group materials by properties and relate properties to uses
prompt: Predict: if a raincoat were made of cotton cloth instead of plastic, what would happen in the rain?
prompt_hi: Guess karo: agar raincoat plastic ki jagah cotton ke kapde ka hota, toh baarish mein kya hota?
answer: Water would soak through the cotton and you would get wet; plastic is waterproof, so it keeps water out.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can group materials by properties and relate properties to uses
prompt: You said the handle stays cool. Then why is the pan itself made of metal and not plastic?
prompt_hi: Tumne kaha handle thanda rehta hai. Toh kadhai khud dhaatu ki kyon hoti hai, plastic ki kyon nahi?
answer: Heat passes through metal quickly to cook the food, and metal doesn't melt on the stove; plastic would melt or burn and passes heat poorly.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can group materials by properties and relate properties to uses
prompt: A steel spoon and a wooden spoon are the same object made of different materials. Name one property where they differ and one job each is better for.
prompt_hi: Steel ki chammach aur lakdi ki chammach, object ek hi hai par material alag. Ek property batao jisme farak hai, aur ek kaam jiske liye har ek behtar hai.
answer: For example: heat passes through steel easily (it gets hot in hot dal) but not through wood; wood is better for stirring hot food in a pan, steel is better for eating and easy to clean. Steel is shiny and wood is dull.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can group materials by properties and relate properties to uses
prompt: Why are school benches usually made of wood or metal, and never of glass?
prompt_hi: School ki bench aam taur pe lakdi ya dhaatu ki kyon hoti hai, kaanch ki kabhi kyon nahi?
answer: Wood and metal are strong and don't break easily; glass breaks easily and the sharp pieces would be dangerous.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can group materials by properties and relate properties to uses
prompt: You are choosing a water bottle for a school trip where it might get dropped. Which material would you choose, and why?
prompt_hi: School trip ke liye paani ki botal chun rahe ho, jahan woh gir sakti hai. Kaunsa material chunoge, aur kyon?
answer: Steel or strong food-safe plastic, because they don't break when dropped and don't leak; glass would break.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can group materials by properties and relate properties to uses
prompt: Draw a Venn diagram with two circles, 'Shiny' and 'Floats on water'. Place a steel spoon, a wooden block, a shiny plastic ball and a stone.
prompt_hi: Do gol ghero wala Venn diagram banao, 'Chamakdaar' aur 'Paani pe tairta hai'. Usme steel ki chammach, lakdi ka block, chamakdaar plastic ki ball aur patthar rakho.
answer: Shiny only: steel spoon. Floats only: wooden block. Both: shiny plastic ball. Outside both: stone.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can group materials by properties and relate properties to uses
prompt: Golu's list of 'materials' is: chair, wood, bottle, plastic, spoon, steel. What is wrong with his list?
prompt_hi: Golu ki 'materials' ki list hai: kursi, lakdi, botal, plastic, chammach, steel. Uski list mein kya galat hai?
answer: Chair, bottle and spoon are objects, not materials; the materials in his list are wood, plastic and steel.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can group materials by properties and relate properties to uses
prompt: Explain why a pressure cooker's body is metal but its handles are plastic, using the words material, property and use.
prompt_hi: Samjhao ki pressure cooker ka body dhaatu ka aur handle plastic ke kyon hote hain, 'material', 'property' aur 'use' shabd use karke.
answer: Key ideas: the body's material is metal, whose property is that heat passes through it quickly and it doesn't melt, so its use is cooking food; the handles' material is plastic, whose property is that heat doesn't pass through it easily, so its use is safe holding.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can group materials by properties and relate properties to uses
prompt: From last time: is steel an object or a material? Name two objects made from it.
prompt_hi: Pichhli baar se: steel object hai ya material? Usse bani do cheezein batao.
answer: A material; e.g. a spoon, tumbler, almirah or plate.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can explain why touch is not reliable for hotness and use temperature in °C
prompt: What do we use to measure temperature, and in what unit?
prompt_hi: Temperature naapne ke liye kya use karte hain, aur kis unit mein?
answer: A thermometer; degrees Celsius (°C).

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can explain why touch is not reliable for hotness and use temperature in °C
prompt: Why can't we always trust our hand to tell how hot something is?
prompt_hi: Hum hamesha apne haath pe bharosa kyon nahi kar sakte ki koi cheez kitni garam hai?
answer: What we feel depends on how warm or cold our hand already is; touch gives no number, and it is unsafe for very hot things.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can explain why touch is not reliable for hotness and use temperature in °C
prompt: Predict: keep your left hand in cold water and your right hand in comfortably warm water (never hot!) for a minute, then put both hands into the same lukewarm water. How will it feel to each hand?
prompt_hi: Guess karo: left haath thande paani mein aur right haath halke garam paani mein (garam bilkul nahi!) ek minute rakho, phir dono ek hi gungune paani mein daalo. Har haath ko kaisa lagega?
answer: The left (cold) hand will feel the lukewarm water as warm; the right (warm) hand will feel it as cool, even though it is the same water.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can explain why touch is not reliable for hotness and use temperature in °C
prompt: Predict: on a winter morning you touch a steel almirah handle and a wooden door at the same time. Which feels colder? Are they at different temperatures?
prompt_hi: Guess karo: sardi ki subah tum ek saath steel ki almari ka handle aur lakdi ka darwaza chhoote ho. Kaun zyada thanda lagega? Kya dono ka temperature alag hai?
answer: The steel feels colder, but both are at the same room temperature; metal takes heat from your hand faster.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can explain why touch is not reliable for hotness and use temperature in °C
prompt: Think it through (this one is only a thought experiment, don't try it with hot water): which can melt more ice cubes in total before it cools down, one spoonful of hot water or a whole bucket of warm water?
prompt_hi: Sirf socho (ye sirf sochne wala experiment hai, garam paani se try mat karna): thanda hone se pehle kaun zyada barf ke tukde pighla sakta hai, ek chammach garam paani ya poori baalti gunguna paani?
answer: The bucket of warm water: it is at a lower temperature, but there is so much more water that it holds much more heat.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can explain why touch is not reliable for hotness and use temperature in °C
prompt: You said the steel and the wood are at the same temperature. Why does the steel feel colder, then?
prompt_hi: Tumne kaha steel aur lakdi ka temperature same hai. Toh steel zyada thanda kyon lagta hai?
answer: Metal takes heat away from our hand much faster than wood does, so our hand cools faster and the metal feels colder.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can explain why touch is not reliable for hotness and use temperature in °C
prompt: Compare a cup of hot chai and a bucket of warm bathwater. Which has the higher temperature? Which holds more heat?
prompt_hi: Garam chai ka cup aur nahaane ke gungune paani ki baalti compare karo. Kiska temperature zyada hai? Kisme zyada heat hai?
answer: The chai has the higher temperature; the bucket holds more heat because there is far more water.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can explain why touch is not reliable for hotness and use temperature in °C
prompt: Your little brother says the floor tiles are 'colder' than the carpet in the same room. What would you tell him?
prompt_hi: Tumhara chhota bhai kehta hai ki ek hi kamre mein tiles carpet se zyada 'thande' hain. Tum use kya bataoge?
answer: Both are at the same room temperature; the tiles take heat from his feet faster, so they feel colder.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can explain why touch is not reliable for hotness and use temperature in °C
prompt: Why do we wear woollen sweaters in winter? Do sweaters make heat?
prompt_hi: Sardi mein hum woollen sweater kyon pehente hain? Kya sweater garmi banata hai?
answer: No, wool doesn't make heat; it traps air and slows heat leaving our body, so we stay warm.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can explain why touch is not reliable for hotness and use temperature in °C
prompt: Place these on a Celsius number line: ice melting (0 °C), normal body temperature (about 37 °C), water boiling (100 °C), a hot summer afternoon in Delhi (about 45 °C).
prompt_hi: In sab ko Celsius number line pe lagao: barf pighalna (0 °C), shareer ka saamaanya temperature (lagbhag 37 °C), paani ubalna (100 °C), Delhi ki garmi ki dopahar (lagbhag 45 °C).
answer: In order: 0 °C (ice melting), 37 °C (body), 45 °C (Delhi summer), 100 °C (boiling water).

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can explain why touch is not reliable for hotness and use temperature in °C
prompt: Golu says: 'Heat and temperature are the same. A big bucket of warm water has a higher temperature than a small cup of hot chai, because it has more heat.' What is wrong?
prompt_hi: Golu kehta hai: 'Heat aur temperature ek hi hain. Gungune paani ki badi baalti ka temperature garam chai ke chhote cup se zyada hai, kyonki usme zyada heat hai.' Galti kya hai?
answer: Temperature measures how hot something is, and the chai is hotter; the amount of heat also depends on how much water there is. Heat and temperature are different.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can explain why touch is not reliable for hotness and use temperature in °C
prompt: Explain to a younger child why we use a thermometer instead of our hand, using the three-bowl experiment.
prompt_hi: Ek chhote bachche ko teen katori wale experiment se samjhao ki hum haath ki jagah thermometer kyon use karte hain.
answer: Key ideas: a hand from cold water feels lukewarm water as warm, and a hand from warm water feels the same water as cool; so touch depends on the hand and is unreliable (and unsafe for very hot things); a thermometer gives the same number in °C for everyone.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can explain why touch is not reliable for hotness and use temperature in °C
prompt: From last time: at what temperature does pure water freeze, in °C?
prompt_hi: Pichhli baar se: shuddh paani kis temperature pe jamta hai, °C mein?

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can read clinical and laboratory thermometers safely and correctly
prompt: What is the range of a clinical thermometer, and why doesn't it need a bigger range?
prompt_hi: Clinical thermometer ki range kya hai, aur ise isse badi range ki zaroorat kyon nahi?
answer: About 35 °C to 42 °C; human body temperature stays within this range.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can read clinical and laboratory thermometers safely and correctly
prompt: On a lab thermometer there are 10 small divisions between the 20 °C and 30 °C marks. What does each small division stand for?
prompt_hi: Lab thermometer pe 20 °C aur 30 °C ke beech 10 chhote khaane hain. Har chhota khaana kitne ka hai?

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can read clinical and laboratory thermometers safely and correctly
prompt: On a clinical thermometer there are 10 small divisions between 37 °C and 38 °C. The reading is 4 small divisions after 37. What is the temperature?
prompt_hi: Clinical thermometer pe 37 °C aur 38 °C ke beech 10 chhote khaane hain. Reading 37 ke baad 4 khaane aage hai. Temperature kitna hai?

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can read clinical and laboratory thermometers safely and correctly
prompt: Predict: you take a lab thermometer out of warm water and wait 30 seconds before reading it. Will the reading be the same as it was in the water?
prompt_hi: Guess karo: lab thermometer ko garam paani se nikaal ke 30 second baad padho. Kya reading wahi hogi jo paani mein thi?
answer: No; once out of the water it starts changing towards room temperature (it falls if the water was warmer than the room).

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can read clinical and laboratory thermometers safely and correctly
prompt: Predict: can a clinical thermometer show the temperature of cold water from the fridge (about 5 °C)?
prompt_hi: Guess karo: kya clinical thermometer fridge ke thande paani (lagbhag 5 °C) ka temperature dikha sakta hai?
answer: No; its scale starts at about 35 °C, so it can't show 5 °C. Use a lab thermometer.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can read clinical and laboratory thermometers safely and correctly
prompt: You said to read the lab thermometer while it's still in the water. Why?
prompt_hi: Tumne kaha lab thermometer ko paani ke andar rehte hue hi padho. Kyon?
answer: Once it's out, it starts gaining or losing heat to the air and the reading changes, giving a wrong value.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can read clinical and laboratory thermometers safely and correctly
prompt: Compare a clinical thermometer and a laboratory thermometer: range, use and one special feature.
prompt_hi: Clinical aur laboratory thermometer compare karo: range, use aur ek khaas baat.
answer: Clinical: about 35-42 °C, for body temperature; a mercury one has a kink so the reading stays until shaken, and digital ones beep when done. Lab: about −10 to 110 °C, for liquids and experiments; no kink, so it must be read while in the liquid.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can read clinical and laboratory thermometers safely and correctly
prompt: A digital thermometer shows 101.3 °F for your sister. Normal is about 98.6 °F. Does she have a fever?
prompt_hi: Digital thermometer tumhari behen ka 101.3 °F dikhata hai. Normal lagbhag 98.6 °F hai. Kya use bukhaar hai?
answer: Yes; it is about 2.7 °F above normal (about 38.5 °C), which is a fever, so tell an adult.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can read clinical and laboratory thermometers safely and correctly
prompt: Your science-fair team wants to record how fast hot water cools in a steel tumbler and in a clay kulhad (a teacher or other adult pours the hot water). Which thermometer will you use, and what are two rules for reading it correctly?
prompt_hi: Tumhari science fair team record karna chahti hai ki garam paani steel ke tumbler aur mitti ke kulhad mein kitni jaldi thanda hota hai (garam paani teacher ya koi bada hi daalega). Kaunsa thermometer use karoge, aur sahi padhne ke do niyam batao.
answer: A laboratory thermometer (an adult pours the hot water). Rules (any two): keep the bulb in the water without touching the bottom or sides; keep it upright; read while it's still in the water; keep your eye level with the top of the column.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can read clinical and laboratory thermometers safely and correctly
prompt: Draw a lab thermometer scale from 20 °C to 40 °C with a mark at every 1 °C. Shade the liquid up to 33 °C. How many small divisions above 30 °C did you shade?
prompt_hi: 20 °C se 40 °C tak lab thermometer ka scale banao, har 1 °C pe nishaan. 33 °C tak liquid ko rang do. 30 °C ke upar kitne chhote khaane rangeen kiye?
answer: 3 divisions above 30 °C.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can read clinical and laboratory thermometers safely and correctly
prompt: Golu wants to check if the chai is too hot by dipping the family's clinical thermometer in it. What is the problem, and what should be used instead?
prompt_hi: Golu ghar ke clinical thermometer ko chai mein daal ke dekhna chahta hai ki chai zyada garam hai ya nahi. Dikkat kya hai, aur iski jagah kya use karna chahiye?
answer: Chai is far above 42 °C, so a clinical thermometer can't measure it and may break (mercury ones release poisonous mercury); a lab thermometer should be used, with an adult's help.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can read clinical and laboratory thermometers safely and correctly
prompt: Teach your cousin how to take someone's temperature correctly with a clinical thermometer, with an adult helping.
prompt_hi: Apne cousin ko sikhao ki clinical thermometer se kisi ka temperature sahi kaise lete hain, kisi bade ki madad se.
answer: Key ideas: an adult helps; a digital thermometer is safest for children; clean it; for a mercury type, an adult shakes it until it reads below 35 °C; place it in the armpit (for children, armpit is safer than the mouth, since a glass one can break); wait the full time (a few minutes in the armpit, or until a digital one beeps); read it holding it at eye level; clean it again; normal is about 37 °C (an armpit reading is a little lower).

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can read clinical and laboratory thermometers safely and correctly
prompt: From last time: what is normal human body temperature in °C?
prompt_hi: Pichhli baar se: insaan ke shareer ka saamaanya temperature °C mein kitna hota hai?
answer: About 37 °C.

subject: science
chapter: A Journey through States of Water
topic: Solid, liquid and gas states of water
outcomes: Learner can describe the three states of water and changes between them
prompt: Name the three states of water and give one example of each from your home.
prompt_hi: Paani ki teen avasthaayein batao aur har ek ka ghar se ek example do.
answer: Solid: ice (ice cubes in the freezer). Liquid: water (from the tap, in a lota). Gas: water vapour (invisible; it rises from wet clothes drying and from boiling water).

subject: science
chapter: A Journey through States of Water
topic: Solid, liquid and gas states of water
outcomes: Learner can describe the three states of water and changes between them
prompt: What do we call (a) ice turning into water, (b) water turning into ice, (c) water vapour turning into water?
prompt_hi: Inhe kya kehte hain: (a) barf ka paani banna, (b) paani ka barf banna, (c) bhaap ka paani banna?
answer: (a) Melting, (b) freezing, (c) condensation.

subject: science
chapter: A Journey through States of Water
topic: Solid, liquid and gas states of water
outcomes: Learner can describe the three states of water and changes between them
prompt: Predict: you pour a glass of water into a flat plate, then from the plate into a tall bottle. Does the amount of water change? Does its shape change?
prompt_hi: Guess karo: ek glass paani ko pehle chapti plate mein daalo, phir plate se lambi botal mein. Kya paani ki matra badlegi? Kya uska aakaar badlega?
answer: The shape changes to fit each container, but the amount (volume) of water stays the same.

subject: science
chapter: A Journey through States of Water
topic: Solid, liquid and gas states of water
outcomes: Learner can describe the three states of water and changes between them
prompt: Predict: an ice cube in a glass and a spoon of sugar stirred into a glass of water both 'disappear'. Is it the same kind of change?
prompt_hi: Guess karo: glass mein rakha ice cube aur paani mein ghuli ek chammach cheeni, dono 'gayab' ho jaate hain. Kya dono ek hi tarah ka badlaav hai?
answer: No. The ice melts: a solid becomes a liquid because of warmth, and it is still water. The sugar dissolves: it spreads into the water to form a sugar solution; it hasn't melted.

subject: science
chapter: A Journey through States of Water
topic: Solid, liquid and gas states of water
outcomes: Learner can describe the three states of water and changes between them
prompt: Predict: you fill an ice tray right to the top with water and freeze it. Will the ice be level with the top, below it, or bulging above it?
prompt_hi: Guess karo: ice tray ko bilkul upar tak paani se bhar ke jamao. Barf upar ke kinare ke barabar hogi, neeche hogi, ya upar ubhri hogi?
answer: It bulges slightly above the top, because water expands when it freezes.

subject: science
chapter: A Journey through States of Water
topic: Solid, liquid and gas states of water
outcomes: Learner can describe the three states of water and changes between them
prompt: Why does an ice cube float in a glass of water?
prompt_hi: Ice cube paani ke glass mein tairta kyon hai?
answer: Water expands when it freezes, so ice is lighter than the same volume of water, and it floats.

subject: science
chapter: A Journey through States of Water
topic: Solid, liquid and gas states of water
outcomes: Learner can describe the three states of water and changes between them
prompt: Watching from a safe distance, compare the clear gap right at a kettle's spout with the white cloud a little above it. Which is water vapour, and what is the white cloud?
prompt_hi: Door se, safely dekhte hue, ketli ki tonti ke theek paas ki saaf jagah aur thoda upar ka safed baadal compare karo. Bhaap (water vapour) kaunsi hai, aur safed baadal kya hai?
answer: The clear gap is invisible water vapour; the white cloud is tiny water droplets formed as the vapour cools in the air and condenses.

subject: science
chapter: A Journey through States of Water
topic: Solid, liquid and gas states of water
outcomes: Learner can describe the three states of water and changes between them
prompt: Kulfi left on the table becomes liquid. You put it back in the freezer and it becomes solid again. Name both changes.
prompt_hi: Mez pe chhodi kulfi paani-paani ho jaati hai. Use wapas freezer mein rakho toh phir se jam jaati hai. Dono badlaavon ke naam batao.
answer: Melting, then freezing.

subject: science
chapter: A Journey through States of Water
topic: Solid, liquid and gas states of water
outcomes: Learner can describe the three states of water and changes between them
prompt: In Ladakh in winter, lakes freeze on top but fish survive below. How is this possible?
prompt_hi: Ladakh mein sardi mein jheelon ki upar ki sateh jam jaati hai, par machhliyan neeche zinda rehti hain. Ye kaise mumkin hai?
answer: Ice is lighter, so it forms and floats on top; this layer of ice works like a lid that keeps the water below from freezing, so the water underneath stays liquid and the fish live there.

subject: science
chapter: A Journey through States of Water
topic: Solid, liquid and gas states of water
outcomes: Learner can describe the three states of water and changes between them
prompt: Draw ice, water and water vapour at the corners of a triangle. Label each arrow between them with the name of the change.
prompt_hi: Ek triangle ke teen konon pe barf, paani aur bhaap banao. Inke beech ke har teer pe badlaav ka naam likho.
answer: Ice → water: melting; water → ice: freezing; water → vapour: evaporation or boiling; vapour → water: condensation.

subject: science
chapter: A Journey through States of Water
topic: Solid, liquid and gas states of water
outcomes: Learner can describe the three states of water and changes between them
prompt: Golu says: 'When water boils, the bubbles are air going in, and the white steam I see is water vapour.' Find both mistakes.
prompt_hi: Golu kehta hai: 'Paani ubalne pe bulbule hawa ke hote hain jo andar jaati hai, aur jo safed bhaap dikhti hai woh water vapour hai.' Dono galtiyan dhundho.
answer: 1) The big bubbles are water vapour forming inside the water, not air. 2) The white cloud is tiny water droplets; real water vapour is invisible.

subject: science
chapter: A Journey through States of Water
topic: Solid, liquid and gas states of water
outcomes: Learner can describe the three states of water and changes between them
prompt: Explain to a younger child the difference between melting and dissolving, using ice and sugar.
prompt_hi: Ek chhote bachche ko barf aur cheeni ke example se pighalne aur ghulne ka farak samjhao.
answer: Key ideas: melting is one substance changing from solid to liquid when warmed (ice → water, still water); dissolving is a solid spreading into a liquid to make a solution (sugar in water); two different changes.

subject: science
chapter: A Journey through States of Water
topic: Solid, liquid and gas states of water
outcomes: Learner can describe the three states of water and changes between them

subject: science
chapter: A Journey through States of Water

prompt_hi: Condensation (sanghanan) kya hai? Ek example do.
answer: Water vapour cooling and changing into liquid droplets; e.g. drops outside a cold glass, mist on a mirror, dew on grass.

subject: science

answer: Tiny water drops; water vapour in the air condenses on the cold surface.

subject: science
chapter: A Journey through States of Water

answer: It evaporates and the plate becomes dry, even though the water never boiled.

subject: science
chapter: A Journey through States of Water

prompt_hi: Guess karo: tum ek thandi steel plate pe aur phir ek garam plate pe phoonk maarte ho. Kis pe dhundhla nishaan zyada saaf dikhega?
answer: On the cold plate; the water vapour in your warm breath condenses on the cool surface.

subject: science
chapter: A Journey through States of Water

prompt_hi: Tumne kaha thandi botal ke bahar ki boondein saaf hoti hain chahe andar rangeen ho. Woh botal ke andar se kyon nahi aa sakti?
answer: The bottle is sealed and the drink can't pass through it; the drops come from water vapour in the surrounding air that cools on the bottle and condenses.

subject: science
chapter: A Journey through States of Water
outcomes: Learner can explain evaporation and condensation using everyday examples
prompt: Compare boiling and evaporation: when and where does each happen?
prompt_hi: Ubalna aur evaporation compare karo: dono kab aur kahan hote hain?
answer: Boiling happens at about 100 °C, all through the water with bubbles, and needs strong heating. Evaporation happens at any temperature, slowly, only from the surface.

subject: science
chapter: A Journey through States of Water
outcomes: Learner can explain evaporation and condensation using everyday examples
prompt: On winter mornings you see tiny drops on grass and on car windscreens. Where did they come from?
prompt_hi: Sardi ki subah ghaas aur gaadi ke sheeshe pe chhoti boondein dikhti hain. Ye kahan se aayin?
answer: This is dew: water vapour in the air condensed on surfaces that cooled down during the cold night.

subject: science
chapter: A Journey through States of Water
outcomes: Learner can explain evaporation and condensation using everyday examples
prompt: Explain how water from the Bay of Bengal can end up as rain on a farm in Odisha.
prompt_hi: Samjhao ki Bay of Bengal ka paani Odisha ke kisi khet pe baarish banke kaise pahunch sakta hai.
answer: The sun warms the sea water and it evaporates into water vapour; the vapour rises, cools and condenses into tiny droplets that form clouds; winds carry the clouds over land; the droplets join and fall as rain.

subject: science
chapter: A Journey through States of Water
outcomes: Learner can explain evaporation and condensation using everyday examples
prompt: Draw the water cycle with arrows: sea, sun, clouds, rain, river. Label evaporation and condensation.
prompt_hi: Teer ke saath water cycle banao: samundar, suraj, baadal, baarish, nadi. Evaporation aur condensation likho.
answer: Sea → (evaporation) vapour rises → (condensation) clouds → rain on land → rivers → back to the sea.

subject: science
chapter: A Journey through States of Water
outcomes: Learner can explain evaporation and condensation using everyday examples
prompt: Golu says: 'Clothes dry only on sunny days, because the sun boils the water out of them.' What is wrong?
prompt_hi: Golu kehta hai: 'Kapde sirf dhoop wale din sookhte hain, kyonki suraj unka paani ubaal deta hai.' Galti kya hai?
answer: Clothes dry on cloudy days too, just more slowly; water evaporates at any temperature without boiling, and the sun only speeds it up.

subject: science
chapter: A Journey through States of Water
outcomes: Learner can explain evaporation and condensation using everyday examples

prompt_hi: Apne dost ko samjhao ki thande nimbu-paani ka glass 'paseena' kyon chhodta hai, aur kaise saabit karoge ki paani andar se nahi nikal raha.
answer: Key ideas: water vapour in the warm air cools on the cold glass and condenses into drops; proof: add colour to the drink and see that the outside drops are clear, or use a sealed bottle that still gets drops.

subject: science
chapter: A Journey through States of Water
outcomes: Learner can explain evaporation and condensation using everyday examples
prompt: From last time: which process forms clouds from water vapour?
prompt_hi: Pichhli baar se: kaunsi prakriya bhaap se baadal banati hai?
answer: Condensation.

subject: science
chapter: A Journey through States of Water

prompt: Name four things that make water evaporate faster.
prompt_hi: Chaar cheezein batao jo paani ko jaldi evaporate karti hain.
answer: Higher temperature (heat or sun), wind (moving air), a larger surface area (spreading the water out) and dry air (low humidity).

subject: science
chapter: A Journey through States of Water
outcomes: Learner can test how temperature, wind and surface area affect evaporation and explain cooling by evaporation
prompt: Why do you feel cooler under a fan on a hot, sweaty day, even though the fan doesn't make the room's air colder?
prompt_hi: Garmi aur paseene wale din pankhe ke neeche thandak kyon lagti hai, jabki pankha kamre ki hawa ko thanda nahi karta?
answer: The moving air makes sweat evaporate faster from your skin, and evaporation takes heat away from the skin, cooling you.

subject: science
chapter: A Journey through States of Water
outcomes: Learner can test how temperature, wind and surface area affect evaporation and explain cooling by evaporation
prompt: Predict: equal amounts of water are put in a wide plate and in a narrow glass, side by side on the same table. Which dries first?
prompt_hi: Guess karo: utna hi paani ek chaudi plate mein aur ek patle glass mein, ek hi mez pe saath rakha. Kaun pehle sookhega?
answer: The wide plate, because the water has a larger surface open to the air.

subject: science
chapter: A Journey through States of Water
outcomes: Learner can test how temperature, wind and surface area affect evaporation and explain cooling by evaporation
prompt: Predict: a matka cools water very well in hot, dry May. Will it cool water as well in humid August during the monsoon? Why?
prompt_hi: Guess karo: garam aur sookhe Mai mein matka paani bahut achha thanda karta hai. Kya umas bhare monsoon ke August mein bhi utna hi thanda karega? Kyon?
answer: Less well; humid air slows evaporation from the pot's surface, so less heat is taken away.

subject: science
chapter: A Journey through States of Water
outcomes: Learner can test how temperature, wind and surface area affect evaporation and explain cooling by evaporation
prompt: Predict: two identical wet handkerchiefs hang in the shade, one under a running fan and one in a still corner. Which dries first?
prompt_hi: Guess karo: chhaon mein do ek jaise geele rumaal, ek chalte pankhe ke neeche aur ek band kone mein. Kaun pehle sookhega?
answer: The one under the fan; moving air speeds up evaporation.

subject: science
chapter: A Journey through States of Water
outcomes: Learner can test how temperature, wind and surface area affect evaporation and explain cooling by evaporation
prompt: You said the plain matka cools better than a fully painted one. Why does that show the clay isn't 'cold' by itself?
prompt_hi: Tumne kaha saada matka paint wale se behtar thanda karta hai. Isse kaise pata chalta hai ki mitti khud 'thandi' nahi hoti?
answer: The painted pot is still clay but cools less, because water can't seep out; the cooling comes from water evaporating from the outer surface, not from the clay.

subject: science
chapter: A Journey through States of Water
outcomes: Learner can test how temperature, wind and surface area affect evaporation and explain cooling by evaporation
prompt: Compare a steel pot and a clay matka filled with the same water in the same room. Which water will be cooler after a few hours, and why?
prompt_hi: Ek hi kamre mein, ek jaise paani se bhara steel ka bartan aur mitti ka matka compare karo. Kuch ghanton baad kiska paani zyada thanda hoga, aur kyon?
answer: The matka's water; water seeps through the matka's pores and evaporates from the outside, cooling it, while the steel pot has no pores, so no water evaporates from its outer surface.

subject: science
chapter: A Journey through States of Water
outcomes: Learner can test how temperature, wind and surface area affect evaporation and explain cooling by evaporation
prompt: When someone has a fever, why might a wet cloth strip on the forehead help them feel cooler?
prompt_hi: Bukhaar mein maathe pe geeli patti rakhne se thandak kyon mil sakti hai?
answer: Water from the cloth evaporates, and evaporation takes heat from the forehead, cooling it.

subject: science
chapter: A Journey through States of Water
outcomes: Learner can test how temperature, wind and surface area affect evaporation and explain cooling by evaporation
prompt: People in hot, dry Rajasthan hang wet khus mats on windows or use desert coolers. Why does this cool the air coming in, and why does it work poorly in humid Kolkata?
prompt_hi: Garam aur sookhe Rajasthan mein log khidki pe geeli khus ki chatai lagaate hain ya desert cooler chalate hain. Isse andar aati hawa thandi kyon hoti hai, aur umas wale Kolkata mein ye kam kyon chalta hai?
answer: Hot, dry air passing through the wet mats makes the water evaporate, which takes heat from the air, so cooler air comes in. In humid air evaporation is slow, so there is much less cooling.

subject: science
chapter: A Journey through States of Water
outcomes: Learner can test how temperature, wind and surface area affect evaporation and explain cooling by evaporation
prompt: Riya's results: same amount of water, same place; a wide plate dried in 2 hours and a cup dried in 6 hours. Show this as a table or bar chart and state the conclusion.
prompt_hi: Riya ke results: utna hi paani, same jagah; chaudi plate 2 ghante mein sookhi aur cup 6 ghante mein. Ise table ya bar chart mein dikhao aur nateeja likho.
answer: Plate: 2 h; cup: 6 h. Conclusion: a larger surface area makes water evaporate faster.

subject: science
chapter: A Journey through States of Water
outcomes: Learner can test how temperature, wind and surface area affect evaporation and explain cooling by evaporation
prompt: Golu tests wind: one wet cloth hangs under a fan in the sun, the other in a shady room with no fan. The fan one dries first, so he says, 'Wind speeds up drying.' What is wrong with his test?
prompt_hi: Golu hawa ka test karta hai: ek geela kapda dhoop mein pankhe ke neeche, doosra chhaon wale kamre mein bina pankhe ke. Pankhe wala pehle sookhta hai, toh woh kehta hai, 'Hawa se jaldi sookhta hai.' Uske test mein kya galat hai?
answer: Two things changed (wind and sunlight or temperature), so he can't tell which one caused it; he should keep both cloths in the shade and change only the fan.

subject: science
chapter: A Journey through States of Water
outcomes: Learner can test how temperature, wind and surface area affect evaporation and explain cooling by evaporation
prompt: Explain to your grandmother, in your own words, how her matka keeps water cool.
prompt_hi: Apni daadi ya naani ko apne shabdon mein samjhao ki unka matka paani thanda kaise rakhta hai.
answer: Key ideas: the clay has tiny pores; some water seeps to the outside; it evaporates from the outer surface; evaporation takes heat from the pot and the water inside, so the water cools; it works best in hot, dry, airy places.

subject: science
chapter: A Journey through States of Water
outcomes: Learner can test how temperature, wind and surface area affect evaporation and explain cooling by evaporation
prompt: From last time: do clothes dry faster on a humid day or on a dry day?
prompt_hi: Pichhli baar se: kapde umas wale din jaldi sookhte hain ya sookhe din?
answer: On a dry day (low humidity).

prompt_hi: Dal ki thali se chhote kankar nikaalne ke liye kaunsa tareeka use karoge?
answer: Handpicking.

subject: science
chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
outcomes: Learner can choose a suitable method to separate mixtures based on differences in size, weight and other properties
prompt: Give two reasons why we separate mixtures.
prompt_hi: Mishran ko alag karne ke do kaaran batao.
answer: To remove harmful or unwanted things (stones, husk, dirt) and to get the useful parts (grain, butter, salt).

subject: science
chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
outcomes: Learner can choose a suitable method to separate mixtures based on differences in size, weight and other properties
prompt: Predict: on a windy day a farmer lets a mixture of wheat grain and husk fall from a height. Where will each land?
prompt_hi: Guess karo: hawa wale din kisaan oonchai se gehun ke daane aur bhoose ka mishran giraata hai. Dono kahan girenge?
answer: The grain is heavier and falls almost straight down near the farmer; the husk is lighter and is blown farther away.

subject: science
chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
outcomes: Learner can choose a suitable method to separate mixtures based on differences in size, weight and other properties
prompt: Predict: you shake a mixture of atta and some small pebbles in a kitchen sieve (chalni). What stays in the sieve and what goes through?
prompt_hi: Guess karo: aate aur kuch chhote kankaron ka mishran chalni mein hilaate ho. Kya chalni mein rahega aur kya neeche girega?
answer: The fine flour passes through; the pebbles (and any bran) stay in the sieve.

subject: science
chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
outcomes: Learner can choose a suitable method to separate mixtures based on differences in size, weight and other properties
prompt: Predict: can winnowing separate rice grains from small stones of the same size? Why or why not?
prompt_hi: Guess karo: kya phatakne se chawal ke daane aur unhi ke size ke chhote kankar alag ho sakte hain? Kyon ya kyon nahi?
answer: Mostly no; both are heavy and fall in about the same place. Use handpicking (by colour and shape) instead.

subject: science
chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
outcomes: Learner can choose a suitable method to separate mixtures based on differences in size, weight and other properties
prompt: You said the husk blows away. Why doesn't the grain blow away too?
prompt_hi: Tumne kaha bhoosa udd jaata hai. Daane bhi kyon nahi udte?
answer: The grain is much heavier, so the wind can't carry it far; the husk is light.

subject: science
chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
outcomes: Learner can choose a suitable method to separate mixtures based on differences in size, weight and other properties
prompt: Compare sieving and winnowing: what difference between the parts does each one use?
prompt_hi: Chhaanna (sieving) aur phatakna (winnowing) compare karo: dono hisson ke beech kaunsa farak use karte hain?
answer: Sieving uses a difference in size; winnowing uses a difference in weight (light versus heavy), with the help of wind.

subject: science
chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
outcomes: Learner can choose a suitable method to separate mixtures based on differences in size, weight and other properties
prompt: At a construction site, workers throw sand onto a slanted wire mesh. What are they doing, and which property are they using?
prompt_hi: Construction site pe mazdoor ret ko tirchhi jaali pe phenkte hain. Woh kya kar rahe hain, aur kaunsi property use kar rahe hain?
answer: Sieving: fine sand passes through the mesh and pebbles and stones roll off; it separates by size.

subject: science
chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
outcomes: Learner can choose a suitable method to separate mixtures based on differences in size, weight and other properties
prompt: Your mother bought a bag of moong that has small stones, some dust and bits of husk in it. Plan the steps to clean it.
prompt_hi: Mummy ne moong ka thaila khareeda jisme chhote kankar, thodi dhool aur bhoose ke tukde hain. Saaf karne ke steps plan karo.
answer: For example: winnow it (with a supa or in a breeze) to remove husk and dust; handpick the stones; sieve if fine dust remains; then wash it. Each step uses a different difference between the parts.

subject: science
chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
outcomes: Learner can choose a suitable method to separate mixtures based on differences in size, weight and other properties
prompt: Draw a winnowing scene: a farmer on a stool, an arrow for the wind, a heap of grain and a heap of husk. Label which heap is closer and why.
prompt_hi: Phatakne ka drishya banao: stool pe khada kisaan, hawa ka teer, anaaj ka dher aur bhoose ka dher. Likho kaunsa dher paas hai aur kyon.
answer: The grain heap is right below and close to the farmer; the husk heap is farther away in the direction of the wind, because husk is lighter.

subject: science
chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
outcomes: Learner can choose a suitable method to separate mixtures based on differences in size, weight and other properties
prompt: Golu says: 'To separate black til from white til of the same size, I'll use a sieve.' What is wrong?
prompt_hi: Golu kehta hai: 'Ek hi size ke kaale til aur safed til ko alag karne ke liye main chalni use karunga.' Galti kya hai?
answer: A sieve separates by size, and the seeds are the same size, so they would all pass through or all stay. Only colour differs, so handpicking is the simple method, though slow.

subject: science
chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
outcomes: Learner can choose a suitable method to separate mixtures based on differences in size, weight and other properties
prompt: Explain to a city friend how grain gets from the field into a clean sack, using threshing and winnowing.
prompt_hi: Shehar ke dost ko samjhao ki anaaj khet se saaf bore tak kaise pahunchta hai, threshing aur winnowing ke saath.
answer: Key ideas: harvested stalks are threshed (beaten, or trampled or machine-crushed) to free the grain; the mixture is winnowed in the wind so the light husk blows away; remaining stones are handpicked or sieved; the clean grain is filled in sacks.

subject: science
chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
outcomes: Learner can choose a suitable method to separate mixtures based on differences in size, weight and other properties
prompt: From last time: what is threshing?
prompt_hi: Pichhli baar se: threshing (gahaai) kya hai?
answer: Beating or crushing harvested stalks to separate the grain from the stalks.

subject: science

prompt: What is decantation?
prompt_hi: Decantation (niraharan) kya hai?
answer: Gently pouring off the clearer liquid on top without disturbing the solid that has settled at the bottom.

subject: science
chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
outcomes: Learner can separate insoluble solids from liquids and dissolved solids by evaporation
prompt: How is tea separated from tea leaves when your family makes chai?
prompt_hi: Ghar pe chai banate waqt chai ko patti se kaise alag karte hain?
answer: By filtration (straining) through a tea strainer: the leaves stay in the strainer and the tea passes through.

subject: science
chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
outcomes: Learner can separate insoluble solids from liquids and dissolved solids by evaporation

prompt_hi: Guess karo: glass mein matmaila paani hila ke ek ghante tak bina chhede rakho. Kya dikhega?
answer: The mud and sand settle at the bottom (sedimentation), with clearer water on top, though it may still be a little cloudy.

subject: science
chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
outcomes: Learner can separate insoluble solids from liquids and dissolved solids by evaporation
prompt: Predict: you pour salt water through a clean cloth or filter paper. Will the water coming out still be salty?
prompt_hi: Guess karo: namak wala paani saaf kapde ya filter paper se chhaano. Jo paani niklega, kya woh ab bhi namkeen hoga?
answer: Yes; the salt is dissolved and passes through the filter with the water.

subject: science
chapter: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
outcomes: Learner can separate insoluble solids from liquids and dissolved solids by evaporation
