outcomes: Learner can explain day-night by rotation and the year by revolution
prompt: How long does the Earth take to rotate once on its axis, and in which direction does it rotate?
prompt_hi: Earth apni axis pe ek baar ghoomne mein kitna samay leti hai, aur kis disha mein ghoomti hai?
answer: About 24 hours, from west to east.

subject: science
topic: Rotation and revolution of the Earth
outcomes: Learner can explain day-night by rotation and the year by revolution
prompt: Why do we have a 29 February only once every four years?
prompt_hi: 29 February chaar saal mein sirf ek baar kyun aati hai?
answer: One revolution takes about 365¼ days; the extra quarter day each year adds up to one full day every four years, which is added as 29 February in a leap year.

subject: science
topic: Rotation and revolution of the Earth
outcomes: Learner can explain day-night by rotation and the year by revolution
prompt: If the Earth is spinning so fast, why do we not feel it moving, and why does the Sun seem to move across the sky instead?
prompt_hi: Agar Earth itni tezi se ghoom rahi hai, toh hum use mehsoos kyun nahi karte, aur ulta Sooraj aasmaan mein chalta kyun dikhta hai?
answer: We move along with the Earth smoothly at a steady speed, so we do not feel it; from the moving Earth, the Sun appears to move from east to west, just as trees seem to move backwards from a smooth-running train.

subject: science
topic: Rotation and revolution of the Earth
outcomes: Learner can explain day-night by rotation and the year by revolution
prompt: Compare rotation and revolution of the Earth: what each is, how long it takes, and what it gives us.
prompt_hi: Earth ke rotation aur revolution ki tulna karo: dono kya hain, kitna samay lete hain, aur humein kya dete hain.
answer: Rotation: spinning on its axis, about 24 hours, gives day and night. Revolution: moving around the Sun, about 365¼ days, gives the year.

subject: science
topic: Rotation and revolution of the Earth
outcomes: Learner can explain day-night by rotation and the year by revolution
prompt: Ishaan says: 'At night the Sun goes under the Earth and comes back up in the morning.' What is wrong?
prompt_hi: Ishaan kehta hai: 'Raat ko Sooraj Earth ke neeche chala jaata hai aur subah wapas upar aata hai.' Kya galat hai?
answer: The Sun does not go around the Earth daily; the Earth rotates, so our side turns away from the Sun at night and back towards it in the morning.

subject: science
topic: Rotation and revolution of the Earth
outcomes: Learner can explain day-night by rotation and the year by revolution
prompt: Draw (or describe) the Earth and Sun from above the North Pole. Mark the day side and night side, and an arrow for the Earth's spin.
prompt_hi: North Pole ke upar se Earth aur Sooraj banao (ya batao). Din wala hissa aur raat wala hissa, aur Earth ke ghoomne ka teer dikhaao.
answer: The half facing the Sun is day; the far half is night; seen from above the North Pole, the Earth spins anticlockwise (west to east).

subject: science
topic: Rotation and revolution of the Earth
outcomes: Learner can explain day-night by rotation and the year by revolution
prompt: Your uncle in New York calls at 8 pm Indian time and says he is having breakfast. Explain how this can be.
prompt_hi: Tumhare chacha New York se Indian time raat 8 baje phone karte hain aur kehte hain ki woh nashta kar rahe hain. Ye kaise ho sakta hai?
answer: New York is on the other side of the Earth; when India has turned away from the Sun (evening/night), New York is turning into sunlight (morning), because the Earth rotates.

subject: science
topic: Rotation and revolution of the Earth
outcomes: Learner can explain day-night by rotation and the year by revolution
prompt: Ancient Indian astronomer Aryabhata wrote that the stars seem to move west because the Earth spins, like stationary objects on the bank seem to move backward to a person in a moving boat. Explain his comparison.
prompt_hi: Prachin bhaarteeya khagolshaastri Aryabhata ne likha ki taare pashchim ki or chalte dikhte hain kyunki Earth ghoomti hai, jaise chalti naav mein baithe insaan ko kinaare ki sthir cheezein peeche jaati dikhti hain. Unki tulna samjhao.
answer: In a moving boat, the still trees on the bank appear to move the opposite way; similarly, as the Earth spins from west to east, the still stars appear to move from east to west.

subject: science
topic: Rotation and revolution of the Earth
outcomes: Learner can explain day-night by rotation and the year by revolution
prompt: Explain to your younger cousin, using a ball and a torch, why we have day and night and why the Sun rises in the east.
prompt_hi: Chhote cousin ko ball aur torch se samjhao ki din aur raat kyun hote hain aur Sooraj poorab mein kyun ugta hai.
answer: Key ideas: the Earth is a ball lit by the Sun on one half; it spins on its axis from west to east in about 24 hours; the lit half has day, the other night; turning eastward into the light makes the Sun appear to rise in the east.

subject: science
topic: Rotation and revolution of the Earth
outcomes: Learner can explain day-night by rotation and the year by revolution
prompt: From memory: how long does the Earth take to go once around the Sun?
prompt_hi: Yaad se batao: Earth ko Sooraj ka ek chakkar lagaane mein kitna samay lagta hai?
answer: About 365¼ days (one year).

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can explain seasons by the tilt of the Earth’s axis
prompt: Shine a torch straight down on squared paper and count roughly how many squares are lit. Then tilt the torch at a slant from the same height. Before you do, predict: will the lit patch get bigger or smaller, brighter or dimmer?
prompt_hi: Torch ko squared paper pe seedha neeche chamkaao aur lagbhag gino kitne khaane roshan hain. Phir usi oonchaai se torch ko tircha karo. Karne se pehle guess karo: roshan hissa bada hoga ya chhota, chamakdaar ya dhundhla?
answer: Bigger and dimmer: the same light spreads over more squares, so each square gets less light and heat, like slanting winter sunlight.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can explain seasons by the tilt of the Earth’s axis
prompt: In June it is summer in Delhi. Predict the season in Sydney, Australia, at the same time, and explain.
prompt_hi: June mein Delhi mein garmi hoti hai. Usi samay Sydney, Australia mein kaunsa mausam hoga, guess karo aur samjhao.
answer: Winter, because in June the southern hemisphere is tilted away from the Sun, getting slanting rays and shorter days.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can explain seasons by the tilt of the Earth’s axis
prompt: By about how many degrees is the Earth's axis tilted?
prompt_hi: Earth ki axis lagbhag kitne degree jhuki hui hai?
answer: About 23.5° (from the perpendicular to its orbit).

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can explain seasons by the tilt of the Earth’s axis
prompt: Why are days longer than nights in Delhi in June?
prompt_hi: June mein Delhi mein din raaton se lambe kyun hote hain?
answer: In June the northern hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun, so places like Delhi spend more of each rotation in the lit half, giving longer days.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can explain seasons by the tilt of the Earth’s axis
prompt: Compare summer and winter in India: the angle of the Sun's rays at noon and the length of the day.
prompt_hi: India mein garmi aur sardi ki tulna karo: dopahar mein Sooraj ki kirnon ka kon aur din ki lambaai.
answer: Summer: the noon Sun is high, rays fall more directly, days are longer. Winter: the noon Sun is lower, rays slant and spread out, days are shorter.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can explain seasons by the tilt of the Earth’s axis
prompt: A website says: 'We have summer because the Earth moves closer to the Sun.' Give two pieces of evidence that this is wrong.
prompt_hi: Ek website kehti hai: 'Garmi isliye hoti hai kyunki Earth Sooraj ke paas aa jaati hai.' Do saboot do ki ye galat hai.
answer: 1) The Earth is closest to the Sun in early January, during northern winter. 2) The two hemispheres have opposite seasons at the same time, which distance cannot explain since both are at the same distance.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can explain seasons by the tilt of the Earth’s axis
prompt: Draw (or describe) the Earth at two places in its orbit, June and December, with the tilted axis. Show which hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun in each.
prompt_hi: Orbit mein do jagah Earth banao (ya batao), June aur December, jhuki axis ke saath. Dikhaao har ek mein kaunsa hemisphere Sooraj ki taraf jhuka hai.
answer: June: the axis tilts the North Pole towards the Sun, so the northern hemisphere is tilted towards it. December (opposite side of the orbit): the axis still points the same way, so now the South Pole side is towards the Sun.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can explain seasons by the tilt of the Earth’s axis
prompt: Near the equator, in places like Singapore, there is little difference between summer and winter. Using the tilt idea, suggest why.
prompt_hi: Bhoomadhya rekha ke paas, jaise Singapore mein, garmi aur sardi mein zyada farak nahi hota. Tilt ke idea se kaaran socho.
answer: Near the equator the Sun is high in the sky all year and day length stays close to 12 hours, so the heating changes little through the year.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can explain seasons by the tilt of the Earth’s axis
prompt: Indian Antarctic stations Maitri and Bharati see the Sun not setting for weeks in December-January. Explain using the tilt.
prompt_hi: Bhaarat ke Antarctic station Maitri aur Bharati par December-January mein hafton tak Sooraj nahi doobta. Tilt se samjhao.
answer: In December-January the southern hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun, so the region near the South Pole stays in the lit half throughout each rotation, giving continuous daylight.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can explain seasons by the tilt of the Earth’s axis
prompt: Explain to a friend, with a ball and a torch, why India has summer in May-June and winter in December-January.
prompt_hi: Ek dost ko ball aur torch se samjhao ki India mein May-June mein garmi aur December-January mein sardi kyun hoti hai.
answer: Key ideas: Earth's axis is tilted and keeps pointing the same way; in May-June the north is tilted towards the Sun, giving direct rays and long days; in December-January it is tilted away, giving slanting rays and short days; distance is not the reason.

subject: science

answer: Early January.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can explain how solar and lunar eclipses occur and how to view them safely
prompt: In a dark room, put a torch (Sun), a small ball (Moon) and a big ball (Earth) in a straight line with the small ball in the middle. Before you look, predict what falls on the big ball.
prompt_hi: Andhere kamre mein torch (Sooraj), chhoti ball (Chaand) aur badi ball (Earth) ek seedhi line mein rakho, chhoti ball beech mein. Dekhne se pehle guess karo badi ball pe kya padega.
answer: The small ball's shadow falls on a small part of the big ball: this models a solar eclipse, seen only from the places where the Moon's shadow falls.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can explain how solar and lunar eclipses occur and how to view them safely
prompt: Now place the big ball (Earth) in the middle, between the torch and the small ball. Predict what happens to the small ball, and which eclipse this is.
prompt_hi: Ab badi ball (Earth) ko beech mein rakho, torch aur chhoti ball ke beech. Guess karo chhoti ball ka kya hoga, aur ye kaunsa grahan hai.
answer: The small ball goes into the big ball's shadow and becomes dark: this models a lunar eclipse.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can explain how solar and lunar eclipses occur and how to view them safely
prompt: With one lamp in a room, hold a ball on a stick at arm's length and slowly turn around on the spot. Predict how much of the lit part of the ball you will see when it is between you and the lamp, and when the lamp is behind you.
prompt_hi: Kamre mein ek lamp ho, ek ball ko danda pe haath bhar door pakdo aur dheere-dheere apni jagah ghoomo. Guess karo ball ka roshan hissa kitna dikhega jab ball tumhare aur lamp ke beech ho, aur jab lamp tumhare peeche ho.
answer: Between you and the lamp: almost none (like a new moon). Lamp behind you (ball held up so your head's shadow does not fall on it): the whole lit face (like a full moon). In between you see partly lit shapes, which are the phases.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can explain how solar and lunar eclipses occur and how to view them safely
prompt: Why does an eclipse not happen every month?
prompt_hi: Har mahine grahan kyun nahi hota?
answer: The Moon's orbit is tilted by about 5° to the Earth's orbit, so in most months the Moon passes a little above or below the line joining the Sun and Earth, and no shadow falls exactly.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can explain how solar and lunar eclipses occur and how to view them safely
prompt: Compare a half moon and a partial lunar eclipse: what causes the dark part in each?

answer: Half moon: we are seeing half of the Moon's sunlit side; the dark part is the Moon's own night side. Partial lunar eclipse: the Earth's shadow is falling on part of the Moon.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can explain how solar and lunar eclipses occur and how to view them safely
prompt: A friend says: 'During a solar eclipse the Sun is covered, so I can look at it with my sunglasses.' Explain why this is dangerous and give a safe method.
prompt_hi: Ek dost kehta hai: 'Surya grahan mein Sooraj dhak jaata hai, toh main sunglasses se dekh sakta hoon.' Samjhao ye khatarnaak kyun hai aur surakshit tareeka batao.
answer: Even the uncovered part of the Sun is bright enough to damage the eyes permanently, and sunglasses do not block enough; use pinhole projection onto paper (looking at the paper, not the Sun) or certified eclipse glasses.

subject: science

prompt_hi: Surya grahan aur chandra grahan ke samay Sooraj, Earth aur Chaand ki sthiti banao (ya batao).
answer: Solar eclipse: Sun, Moon, Earth in a line (Moon in the middle). Lunar eclipse: Sun, Earth, Moon in a line (Earth in the middle).

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can explain how solar and lunar eclipses occur and how to view them safely
prompt: During a total lunar eclipse the Moon often looks a dull coppery red rather than completely black. Is the Moon making its own light now? What is the more likely reason?
prompt_hi: Poore chandra grahan mein Chaand aksar bilkul kaala nahi balki halka taambe jaisa laal dikhta hai. Kya Chaand ab khud roshni de raha hai? Zyada sambhav kaaran kya hai?
answer: No, the Moon is still non-luminous; a little sunlight is bent through the Earth's atmosphere into the shadow, and mostly reddish light gets through (like the red of sunsets), dimly lighting the Moon.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can explain how solar and lunar eclipses occur and how to view them safely
prompt: Your school plans to watch a partial solar eclipse. Using only a sheet of cardboard and a white paper, describe a safe way for everyone to watch it.
prompt_hi: Tumhaara school aanshik surya grahan dekhna chahta hai. Sirf ek gatte aur safed kaagaz se sabke liye surakshit tareeka batao.
answer: Make a small hole in the cardboard; stand with your back to the Sun; let sunlight pass through the hole onto the white paper held a little away; look only at the paper, where a small image of the partly covered Sun appears. Never look at the Sun through the hole.

subject: science
outcomes: Learner can explain how solar and lunar eclipses occur and how to view them safely
prompt: Explain to your family the difference between a solar eclipse, a lunar eclipse and the phases of the Moon.
prompt_hi: Apne parivaar ko surya grahan, chandra grahan aur chaand ki kalaaon ka farak samjhao.
answer: Key ideas: solar eclipse, Moon between Sun and Earth, Moon's shadow on Earth, at new moon, never look directly; lunar eclipse, Earth between Sun and Moon, Earth's shadow on Moon, at full moon, safe to view; phases, how much of the Moon's sunlit half we see, every month, not a shadow; eclipses are rare because the Moon's orbit is tilted.

subject: science

outcomes: Learner can describe India’s major physical regions and how they shape ways of life
prompt: Compare life in a village in Ladakh with life in a village in the Ganga plains: one difference each in crops, houses and travel.
prompt_hi: Ladakh ke ek gaon aur Ganga ke maidan ke ek gaon ki zindagi compare karo: fasal, ghar aur safar mein ek-ek fark batao.
answer: Ladakh: cold, dry, high — barley and apricots, short growing season; flat-roofed stone or mud-brick houses with thick walls; mountain roads and passes closed by snow in winter. Ganga plains: hot summers, fertile flat land — rice, wheat, sugarcane; brick houses, often sloping roofs; easy flat roads and railways.

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can describe India’s major physical regions and how they shape ways of life
prompt: Think about your own town or village. Which physical region is it in? Give two ways the land or rivers there shape what people grow, eat or do for work.
prompt_hi: Apne shehar ya gaon ke baare mein socho. Woh kis physical region mein hai? Do tareeke batao jinse wahan ki zameen ya nadiyaan logon ki kheti, khaana ya kaam-dhandha tay karti hain.
answer: A correct answer names the right region for the child's place and gives two real links between landform/rivers and life (e.g. coastal town → fishing and coconut; plains → wheat and rice farming; plateau → cotton on black soil; hills → terrace farming, tea).

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can describe India’s major physical regions and how they shape ways of life
prompt: Find the mistakes: "The Deccan Plateau is a young mountain range made of soft soil brought by rivers, and its big rivers all flow west."
prompt_hi: Galti dhoondho: "Deccan Pathaar ek nayi parvat shrinkhla hai jo nadiyon ki laayi naram mitti se bani hai, aur iski saari badi nadiyaan pashchim ki taraf behti hain."
answer: The Deccan is an old plateau of hard rock (not a young mountain range of soft river soil); most of its big rivers (Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri, Mahanadi) flow east into the Bay of Bengal — only a few, like the Narmada and Tapi, flow west.

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can describe India’s major physical regions and how they shape ways of life
prompt: On a physical map, one line of hills runs unbroken close to the west coast; another runs broken into pieces along the east. Name each and say why the eastern one is broken.
prompt_hi: Physical map par ek pahadiyon ki line pashchimi tat ke paas bina toote chalti hai; doosri poorab mein tukdon mein bati hai. Dono ke naam batao aur poorvi wali tooti kyun hai?
answer: The unbroken western line is the Western Ghats (Sahyadri); the broken eastern line is the Eastern Ghats, cut through by big east-flowing rivers like the Godavari, Krishna, Mahanadi and Kaveri.

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can describe India’s major physical regions and how they shape ways of life
prompt: Teach a cousin from another country why India is called a land of geographical diversity. Use at least three regions and say how life differs in each.
prompt_hi: Videsh mein rehne wale apne cousin ko samjhao ki India ko bhaugolik vividhta (geographical diversity) wala desh kyun kehte hain. Kam se kam teen regions lo aur batao wahan zindagi kaise alag hai.
answer: Key idea: India has mountains, plains, desert, plateau, coasts and islands side by side; each has different height, soil, rivers and climate, which leads to different crops, homes, food and work.

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can describe India’s major physical regions and how they shape ways of life
prompt: Why do so many people live in the Northern Plains?
prompt_hi: Northern Plains mein itne saare log kyun rehte hain?
answer: The land is flat and fertile with rivers that flow all year, so farming is easy and food is plentiful; flat land also makes roads, railways, towns and trade easy.

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can describe India’s major physical regions and how they shape ways of life
prompt: A trekker starts at Dehradun (about 650 m high) and climbs to a pass about 4,000 m high. Predict: will it get warmer or colder as she climbs? Why?
prompt_hi: Ek trekker Dehradun (lagbhag 650 m) se chal ke lagbhag 4,000 m oonche darre tak chadhti hai. Socho: oopar jaate hue thand badhegi ya garmi? Kyun?
answer: Colder: air temperature falls as height increases (roughly 6 °C for every 1,000 m), so at 4,000 m it is much colder even though she is "closer to the sun".

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can explain elements of weather (temperature, pressure, wind, humidity, rainfall) and how they are measured
prompt: In one line each, what is weather and what is climate?
prompt_hi: Ek-ek line mein batao: weather (mausam) kya hai aur climate (jalvaayu) kya hai?
answer: Weather is the condition of the air at a place for a short time; climate is the average weather of a place over a long time (about 30 years or more).

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can explain elements of weather (temperature, pressure, wind, humidity, rainfall) and how they are measured
prompt: Sort these into weather or climate: (a) It is raining in Pune right now. (b) Rajasthan is dry most of the year. (c) Puri will be windy tomorrow. (d) Shillong has cool summers.
prompt_hi: Inko weather ya climate mein baanto: (a) Pune mein abhi baarish ho rahi hai. (b) Rajasthan saal ke zyaadatar samay sookha rehta hai. (c) Kal Puri mein tez hawa chalegi. (d) Shillong ki garmiyaan thandi hoti hain.
answer: Weather: (a) and (c). Climate: (b) and (d).

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can explain elements of weather (temperature, pressure, wind, humidity, rainfall) and how they are measured
prompt: Match each instrument to what it measures: thermometer, barometer, anemometer, wind vane, rain gauge, hygrometer.
prompt_hi: Har instrument ko uske naap se milao: thermometer, barometer, anemometer, wind vane, rain gauge, hygrometer.
answer: Thermometer – temperature; barometer – air pressure; anemometer – wind speed; wind vane – wind direction; rain gauge – rainfall; hygrometer – humidity.

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can explain elements of weather (temperature, pressure, wind, humidity, rainfall) and how they are measured
prompt: Find the mistakes: "Ravi measured wind speed with a wind vane and rainfall with a thermometer."
prompt_hi: Galti pakdo: "Ravi ne hawa ki speed wind vane se naapi aur baarish thermometer se."
answer: Wind speed is measured with an anemometer (a wind vane shows direction), and rainfall with a rain gauge (a thermometer measures temperature).

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can explain elements of weather (temperature, pressure, wind, humidity, rainfall) and how they are measured
prompt: On a sunny afternoon at the beach, a cool breeze blows from the sea onto the land. Explain why.
prompt_hi: Dhoop wali dopahar ko beach par samundar se zameen ki taraf thandi hawa chalti hai. Kyun?
answer: Land heats up faster than water; warm air over the land rises, creating lower pressure there; cooler, higher-pressure air over the sea moves in to replace it — the sea breeze.

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can explain elements of weather (temperature, pressure, wind, humidity, rainfall) and how they are measured
prompt: Now predict: at night, which way will the breeze blow at the same beach? Why?
prompt_hi: Ab socho: raat ko usi beach par hawa kis taraf chalegi? Kyun?
answer: From the land to the sea (a land breeze), because land cools faster than water at night, so the air over the sea is warmer and rises, making lower pressure over the sea.

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can explain elements of weather (temperature, pressure, wind, humidity, rainfall) and how they are measured
prompt: There are no trees in the middle of the sea, yet strong winds blow there. What does this tell you about what causes wind?
prompt_hi: Beech samundar mein ek bhi ped nahi hota, phir bhi wahan tez hawa chalti hai. Isse hawa ke kaaran ke baare mein kya pata chalta hai?
answer: Trees do not make wind; wind is air moving from areas of high pressure to areas of low pressure, caused by uneven heating by the sun.

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can explain elements of weather (temperature, pressure, wind, humidity, rainfall) and how they are measured
prompt: Tomorrow's forecast card says: Max 38 °C, Min 27 °C, humidity 80%, wind from the south-west at 20 km/h, chance of rain 70%. Say in words what tomorrow will feel like and what you should carry.
prompt_hi: Kal ke forecast card par likha hai: Max 38 °C, Min 27 °C, humidity 80%, hawa dakshin-pashchim se 20 km/h, baarish ki sambhavna 70%. Shabdon mein batao kal kaisa lagega aur kya saath le jaana chahiye.
answer: A hot, sticky (humid) day with a steady breeze from the south-west and a good chance of rain — carry water and an umbrella or raincoat, and wear light clothes.

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can explain elements of weather (temperature, pressure, wind, humidity, rainfall) and how they are measured
prompt: IMD has issued an orange alert for heavy rain in your district. What does an orange alert mean, and what should your family do?
prompt_hi: IMD ne aapke zile ke liye heavy rain ka orange alert diya hai. Orange alert ka matlab kya hai, aur aapke parivaar ko kya karna chahiye?
answer: Orange means "be prepared": severe weather is likely. Keep updated, avoid unnecessary travel, keep torch, water and phone charged, stay away from flooded roads and rivers, and follow official advice. (Green = no warning, yellow = be aware, red = take action.)

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can explain elements of weather (temperature, pressure, wind, humidity, rainfall) and how they are measured
prompt: Compare a December morning in Delhi with a December morning in Chennai: temperature and humidity.
prompt_hi: December ki ek subah Delhi aur Chennai mein compare karo: taapmaan (temperature) aur humidity.
answer: Delhi: cold (often below 10 °C) and often foggy at dawn; the cold air holds much less water vapour overall. Chennai: mild and warm (around 20–25 °C) with much more water vapour in the air (more humid), because it is near the sea and closer to the equator; Chennai may even get rain from the north-east monsoon in December.

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can explain elements of weather (temperature, pressure, wind, humidity, rainfall) and how they are measured
prompt: Plan a one-week weather diary for your home. Which three weather elements could you measure with simple things, and how would you measure each?
prompt_hi: Ghar ke liye ek hafte ki weather diary plan karo. Kaun se teen element tum seedhi-saadi cheezon se naap sakte ho, aur har ek kaise naapoge?
answer: For example: temperature with a thermometer at the same time each day; rainfall by collecting rain in a straight-sided bottle and measuring the depth in mm with a ruler; wind direction with a ribbon or paper vane and a compass; cloud cover by looking at the sky. Record at the same time and place each day.

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can explain elements of weather (temperature, pressure, wind, humidity, rainfall) and how they are measured
prompt: Teach a younger child the difference between weather and climate using the clothes in your cupboard.
prompt_hi: Apne cupboard ke kapdon ka example le kar chhote bachche ko weather aur climate ka fark samjhao.
answer: Key idea: what you choose to wear today depends on the weather (short-term); which clothes your family owns at all — many sweaters or mostly cotton — depends on the climate (long-term pattern).

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can explain elements of weather (temperature, pressure, wind, humidity, rainfall) and how they are measured
prompt: A bottle rain gauge collected 12 mm of rain on Monday and 30 mm on Tuesday. How much rain fell in the two days, and which instrument idea is this?
prompt_hi: Bottle wale rain gauge mein Monday ko 12 mm aur Tuesday ko 30 mm baarish jama hui. Do din mein kitni baarish hui, aur yeh kaunse instrument ka idea hai?
answer: 42 mm of rain in total; this is a rain gauge, which measures rainfall as the depth of water in millimetres.

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can explain elements of weather (temperature, pressure, wind, humidity, rainfall) and how they are measured
prompt: On a sticky, sweaty afternoon in Kolkata it has not rained at all. Explain the difference between humidity and rainfall using this day.
prompt_hi: Kolkata mein ek chipchipi, paseene wali dopahar ko bilkul baarish nahi hui. Is din ka example le kar humidity aur rainfall ka fark samjhao.
answer: Humidity is the amount of invisible water vapour in the air — high humidity makes us feel sticky because sweat dries slowly; rainfall is water actually falling from clouds as drops. A day can be very humid with no rain at all.

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can describe the monsoon and different climatic regions of India and their effect on life
prompt: Name four factors that affect the climate of a place.
prompt_hi: Kisi jagah ki jalvaayu ko prabhaavit karne wale chaar kaaran batao.
answer: Latitude, altitude (height), distance from the sea, and mountains/relief (also winds).

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can describe the monsoon and different climatic regions of India and their effect on life
prompt: Why is the difference between summer and winter temperatures much smaller in Mumbai than in Delhi?
prompt_hi: Mumbai mein garmi aur sardi ke taapmaan ka fark Delhi se kaafi kam kyun hota hai?
answer: Mumbai is on the coast, and the sea heats and cools slowly, keeping it mild all year; Delhi is far inland, so it gets very hot summers and cold winters (an extreme climate).

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can describe the monsoon and different climatic regions of India and their effect on life
prompt: Put these monsoon steps in order: (a) moist winds blow in from the Indian Ocean; (b) the land heats up strongly in summer; (c) winds rise over the Western Ghats, cool and drop rain; (d) low pressure forms over north-west India.
prompt_hi: Monsoon ke in steps ko sahi kram mein lagao: (a) Hind Mahasagar se nam hawayein aati hain; (b) garmi mein zameen bahut garam hoti hai; (c) hawayein Pashchimi Ghat par chadh ke thandi hoti hain aur baarish girati hain; (d) uttar-pashchim India par low pressure banta hai.
answer: b → d → a → c

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can describe the monsoon and different climatic regions of India and their effect on life
prompt: Why is Mawsynram in Meghalaya one of the wettest places on Earth, while Jaisalmer in Rajasthan is very dry?
prompt_hi: Meghalaya ka Mawsynram duniya ki sabse geeli jagahon mein se ek kyun hai, jabki Rajasthan ka Jaisalmer itna sookha kyun?
answer: Moist monsoon winds from the Bay of Bengal are funnelled into the Khasi hills and forced to rise steeply over Mawsynram, so they cool and drop huge amounts of rain. Jaisalmer is far west in the Thar; the winds reaching it carry little moisture and are not forced to rise (the Aravallis lie along the wind's path, not across it), so little rain falls.

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can describe the monsoon and different climatic regions of India and their effect on life
prompt: Predict: if the Western Ghats did not exist, how would rainfall on the Konkan coast and in the interior of Maharashtra change?
prompt_hi: Socho: agar Pashchimi Ghat hota hi nahi, toh Konkan tat aur Maharashtra ke andar ke ilaakon mein baarish kaise badalti?
answer: The Konkan coast would get much less rain, because the winds would not be forced up to cool and drop their moisture; the interior would no longer be in such a strong rain shadow, so rain would be spread more evenly between the coast and the interior.

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can describe the monsoon and different climatic regions of India and their effect on life
prompt: Find the mistakes: "In winter the sea becomes hotter than the land, so moist winds from the sea bring the south-west monsoon to Kerala in December."
prompt_hi: Galti dhoondho: "Sardi mein samundar zameen se zyada garam ho jaata hai, isliye samundar ki nam hawayein December mein Kerala mein south-west monsoon laati hain."
answer: The south-west monsoon comes in summer (it reaches Kerala around the start of June), when the LAND is hotter than the sea. In winter the land is cooler and winds blow from land to sea (north-east); that retreating monsoon brings rain mainly to the Tamil Nadu coast.

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can describe the monsoon and different climatic regions of India and their effect on life
prompt: A rainfall chart for a city shows little rain from June to September but heavy rain from October to December. Which part of India is it probably in, and why?
prompt_hi: Ek shehar ke rainfall chart mein June-September mein kam baarish aur October-December mein bahut baarish dikhti hai. Yeh shayad India ke kis hisse mein hai, aur kyun?
answer: Probably on the Tamil Nadu (Coromandel) coast, e.g. Chennai: it lies in the rain shadow of the Western Ghats during the south-west monsoon, and gets most rain from the retreating (north-east) monsoon in October–December.

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can describe the monsoon and different climatic regions of India and their effect on life
prompt: Compare the climates of Leh (Ladakh) and Thiruvananthapuram (Kerala), and give one way homes differ.
prompt_hi: Leh (Ladakh) aur Thiruvananthapuram (Kerala) ki jalvaayu compare karo, aur gharon mein ek fark batao.
answer: Leh: very high, cold and dry, freezing winters, very little rain — thick walls, flat roofs, small windows to keep warm. Thiruvananthapuram: low, coastal, warm and humid all year, heavy monsoon rain — sloping roofs to shed rain, open, airy houses.

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can describe the monsoon and different climatic regions of India and their effect on life
prompt: Why do farmers in much of India wait for the monsoon before sowing rice?
prompt_hi: India ke kai hisson mein kisaan dhaan (rice) bone se pehle monsoon ka intezaar kyun karte hain?
answer: Rice needs a lot of water, and in many areas monsoon rain is the main source of water for the fields (kharif season).

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can describe the monsoon and different climatic regions of India and their effect on life
prompt: Describe your own town's climate across the year: the hottest months, the rainiest months, and one festival or food that fits a season.
prompt_hi: Apne shehar ki saal bhar ki jalvaayu batao: sabse garam mahine, sabse zyada baarish wale mahine, aur ek tyohaar ya khaana jo kisi mausam se juda ho.
answer: A correct answer matches the child's region (e.g. north India: hottest April–June, rain July–September, winter December–January) and links a festival or food to a season (e.g. Makar Sankranti or Pongal with harvest, mangoes in summer, hot pakoras in the rains).

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can describe the monsoon and different climatic regions of India and their effect on life
prompt: How is climate change affecting India? Give two effects and one thing families or schools can do.
prompt_hi: Climate change India ko kaise prabhaavit kar raha hai? Do asar batao aur ek cheez jo parivaar ya school kar sakte hain.
answer: Effects: more frequent heatwaves, very heavy rain and floods in short bursts, an erratic monsoon that hurts farming, and shrinking Himalayan glaciers. Actions: save electricity and water, plant and protect trees, use public transport or cycles, reduce waste.

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can describe the monsoon and different climatic regions of India and their effect on life
prompt: Two towns are at the same latitude: one on the coast at sea level, one in the hills at 2,000 m. Predict which is cooler in summer and why.
prompt_hi: Do shehar ek hi latitude par hain: ek samundar kinare (sea level par), ek pahadon mein 2,000 m oonchai par. Garmi mein kaun zyada thanda hoga aur kyun?
answer: The hill town at 2,000 m is cooler, because temperature falls as altitude increases.

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can describe the monsoon and different climatic regions of India and their effect on life
prompt: Teach a friend how the monsoon works, using the idea of beach sand and sea water on a hot day.
prompt_hi: Garam din par beach ki ret aur samundar ke paani ka example le kar dost ko samjhao ki monsoon kaise kaam karta hai.
answer: Key idea: land (like sand) heats faster than the sea; hot air over the land rises and creates low pressure; moist winds from the sea blow in; when they rise over hills they cool and rain falls; in winter the pattern reverses.

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can describe the emergence of janapadas and mahajanapadas and early cities
prompt: Around which century BCE did the mahajanapadas emerge?
prompt_hi: Mahajanapada lagbhag kis shatabdi BCE mein ubhre?
answer: Around the 6th century BCE (about 600 BCE).

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can describe the emergence of janapadas and mahajanapadas and early cities
prompt: Put these in order from earliest to latest: Mahajanapadas emerge (c. 600 BCE); Constitution of India comes into force (1950 CE); Harappan cities at their height (c. 2600 BCE); Chandragupta Maurya founds an empire (c. 321 BCE).
prompt_hi: Inko sabse pehle se sabse baad ke kram mein lagao: Mahajanapada ubharte hain (lagbhag 600 BCE); Bharat ka Samvidhan laagu hota hai (1950 CE); Harappa ke shehar charam par (lagbhag 2600 BCE); Chandragupta Maurya samrajya banate hain (lagbhag 321 BCE).
answer: Harappan cities (c. 2600 BCE) → Mahajanapadas (c. 600 BCE) → Chandragupta Maurya (c. 321 BCE) → Constitution (1950 CE).

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can describe the emergence of janapadas and mahajanapadas and early cities
prompt: Find the mistake: "Rajagriha's wall was built in 500 BCE, so it is older than a coin made in 600 BCE."
prompt_hi: Galti pakdo: "Rajagriha ki deewar 500 BCE mein bani, isliye woh 600 BCE mein bane sikke se purani hai."
answer: Wrong way round: 600 BCE is earlier than 500 BCE, so the 600 BCE coin would be about 100 years older than the 500 BCE wall.

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can describe the emergence of janapadas and mahajanapadas and early cities
prompt: What does the word "janapada" mean?
prompt_hi: "Janapada" shabd ka matlab kya hai?
answer: The land where a jana (a people or clan) set foot and settled.

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can describe the emergence of janapadas and mahajanapadas and early cities
prompt: Name three mahajanapadas and their capitals.
prompt_hi: Teen mahajanapada aur unki rajdhaniyon ke naam batao.
answer: For example: Magadha – Rajagriha (later Pataliputra); Kosala – Shravasti; Vatsa – Kaushambi; Avanti – Ujjayini; Vajji – Vaishali; Gandhara – Takshashila (Taxila); Kashi – Varanasi.

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can describe the emergence of janapadas and mahajanapadas and early cities
prompt: On a map, Magadha sits on the Ganga plains in south Bihar, with rivers around it and hills around Rajagriha. Describe in words two map features that helped Magadha grow strong.
prompt_hi: Map par Magadha dakshin Bihar ke Ganga maidan mein hai, aas-paas nadiyaan hain aur Rajagriha ke chaaron taraf pahadiyaan. Shabdon mein do aisi map wali cheezein batao jinse Magadha shaktishaali bana.
answer: Rivers (like the Ganga and Son) gave water for farming, transport for trade and natural protection; the fertile plains grew plenty of food; the hills around Rajagriha acted as a natural defence wall.

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can describe the emergence of janapadas and mahajanapadas and early cities
prompt: Compare a mahajanapada ruled by a raja with a gana-sangha like the Vajjis: who decided, and how?
prompt_hi: Raja wale mahajanapada aur Vajji jaise gana-sangha ki tulna karo: faisla kaun leta tha, aur kaise?
answer: In a kingdom, one raja (often from one family) made the main decisions, collected taxes and led the army. In a gana-sangha, a group of leaders met in an assembly, discussed and decided together.

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can describe the emergence of janapadas and mahajanapadas and early cities
prompt: Think of how decisions are made in your school or housing society. Is it more like a raja or a gana-sangha? Explain.
prompt_hi: Socho aapke school ya society mein faisle kaise hote hain. Kya woh zyada raja jaisa hai ya gana-sangha jaisa? Samjhao.
answer: A good answer identifies who decides (e.g. a principal alone, or an elected committee that meets and votes) and correctly labels it as more like a raja (one person decides) or a gana-sangha (a group decides together in a meeting).

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can describe the emergence of janapadas and mahajanapadas and early cities
prompt: Why did the spread of iron tools help cities to grow?
prompt_hi: Lohe ke auzaaron ke failne se shehar badhne mein madad kyun mili?
answer: Iron axes and ploughs helped clear forests and farm more land, so farmers grew more food than they needed (a surplus); this extra food could feed people in towns — craftspeople, traders, soldiers and officials.

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can describe the emergence of janapadas and mahajanapadas and early cities
prompt: Predict: if farmers had grown only just enough food for their own families, what would have happened to cities, crafts and armies?
prompt_hi: Socho: agar kisaan sirf apne parivaar jitna hi anaaj ugaate, toh shehron, kaarigaron aur senaon ka kya hota?
answer: Cities, crafts and armies could not have grown, because there would be no extra food to feed people who did not farm, and no surplus for rulers to tax.

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can describe the emergence of janapadas and mahajanapadas and early cities
prompt: An archaeologist finds a small, bent piece of silver stamped with symbols like a sun and a wheel, but no king's name. What is it probably, and what does it tell us?
prompt_hi: Ek archaeologist ko chaandi ka ek chhota, muda hua tukda milta hai jis par suraj aur pahiye jaise nishaan thape hain, par kisi raja ka naam nahi. Yeh shayad kya hai, aur isse kya pata chalta hai?
answer: Probably a punch-marked coin, among the earliest coins in India; it tells us that people were buying and selling with money, so trade was growing in this period.

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can describe the emergence of janapadas and mahajanapadas and early cities
prompt: Teach a friend how a small janapada could become a powerful mahajanapada with a city capital. Use Magadha as your example.
prompt_hi: Dost ko samjhao ki ek chhota janapada kaise ek shaktishaali mahajanapada ban sakta tha jiski rajdhani ek shehar ho. Magadha ka example lo.
answer: Key idea: a jana settles (janapada); with iron tools and fertile land it grows a surplus; rulers collect taxes, build forts and armies, conquer neighbours and become a mahajanapada; trade and crafts make the fortified capital (Rajagriha, later Pataliputra) a city.

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can describe the emergence of janapadas and mahajanapadas and early cities
prompt: Why did rajas build strong walls around their capitals and collect taxes?
prompt_hi: Raja apni rajdhaniyon ke chaaron taraf mazboot deewarein kyun banwaate the aur kar (tax) kyun lete the?
answer: Walls protected the city, its people and its wealth from attacks by rival kingdoms; taxes paid for the army, the walls, officials and the king's court.

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can explain how the Mauryan empire rose and how it was governed, including Ashoka’s dhamma
prompt: Give four reasons why Magadha became so powerful.
prompt_hi: Chaar kaaran batao ki Magadha itna shaktishaali kyun bana.
answer: Fertile Ganga plains, rivers for transport and defence, iron ore for tools and weapons, forests with elephants for the army (also: ambitious rulers and well-protected capitals).

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can explain how the Mauryan empire rose and how it was governed, including Ashoka’s dhamma
prompt: Pataliputra was built where the Ganga and Son rivers meet. Why was this a smart place for a capital?
prompt_hi: Pataliputra wahan bana jahan Ganga aur Son nadiyaan milti hain. Rajdhani ke liye yeh samajhdaari ki jagah kyun thi?
answer: The rivers gave water for farming, easy boat transport for trade and moving armies, and acted as natural moats that made the city harder to attack.

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can explain how the Mauryan empire rose and how it was governed, including Ashoka’s dhamma
prompt: Order these from earliest to latest: Kalinga war; Chandragupta Maurya founds the empire; Bindusara becomes king; Alexander reaches north-west India (326 BCE).

answer: Alexander reaches the north-west (326 BCE) → Chandragupta founds the empire (c. 321 BCE) → Bindusara becomes king (c. 297 BCE) → Kalinga war (c. 261 BCE).

subject: sst

prompt_hi: Chandragupta Maurya ko satta tak pahunchne mein kisne madad ki, aur unse kaunsa prasiddh granth juda hai?
answer: Chanakya (also called Kautilya); the Arthashastra, a text on running a state.

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can explain how the Mauryan empire rose and how it was governed, including Ashoka’s dhamma
prompt: Name three ways the Mauryas kept control over such a huge empire.
prompt_hi: Teen tareeke batao jinse Mauryon ne itne bade samrajya par niyantran rakha.
answer: Dividing it into provinces run by princes or governors; appointing officials and tax collectors; keeping a large army; using spies to report what was happening; building roads to connect regions.

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can explain how the Mauryan empire rose and how it was governed, including Ashoka’s dhamma
prompt: Ashoka's edicts have been found from Kandahar in Afghanistan to Karnataka in the south, and from Gujarat to Odisha. Describe in words what this spread of find-spots on a map tells us.
prompt_hi: Ashoka ke shilalekh Afghanistan ke Kandahar se dakshin mein Karnataka tak, aur Gujarat se Odisha tak mile hain. Shabdon mein batao ki map par yeh failaav humein kya batata hai.
answer: The empire (or at least Ashoka's reach and messages) stretched across most of the subcontinent — from the north-west to the south and from west to east; only the far south lay outside it.

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can explain how the Mauryan empire rose and how it was governed, including Ashoka’s dhamma
prompt: Why did Ashoka change his way of ruling after the Kalinga war?
prompt_hi: Kalinga yuddh ke baad Ashoka ne raaj karne ka tareeka kyun badla?
answer: He saw the huge suffering — deaths, injuries and people taken from their homes — and, as he wrote himself, felt deep regret; he gave up wars of conquest and chose to rule through dhamma.

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can explain how the Mauryan empire rose and how it was governed, including Ashoka’s dhamma
prompt: Compare how Chandragupta built his empire with how Ashoka ruled after Kalinga.
prompt_hi: Chandragupta ne samrajya kaise banaya aur Kalinga ke baad Ashoka ne kaise raaj kiya — tulna karo.
answer: Chandragupta built it by conquest, a strong army and careful statecraft (advised by Chanakya). After Kalinga, Ashoka kept the empire but stopped wars of conquest, ruled through dhamma, sent officials to spread its message, and cared for people's welfare (wells, rest houses, care for animals).

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can explain how the Mauryan empire rose and how it was governed, including Ashoka’s dhamma
prompt: Find the mistakes: "Ashoka's edicts were written in English on paper and posted to every village."
prompt_hi: Galti dhoondho: "Ashoka ke shilalekh angrezi mein kaagaz par likh kar har gaon mein bheje gaye."
answer: They were carved on rocks and stone pillars (not paper), mostly in Prakrit using the Brahmi script (some in the north-west in Greek, Aramaic and Kharosthi) — English did not exist then.

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can explain how the Mauryan empire rose and how it was governed, including Ashoka’s dhamma
prompt: Where in your daily life do you see a symbol from Ashoka's time? And what one message would you carve on a "dhamma pillar" at your school today?
prompt_hi: Roz ki zindagi mein Ashoka ke zamaane ka koi nishaan tum kahan dekhte ho? Aur aaj apne school ke "dhamma stambh" par tum kaunsa ek sandesh likhoge?
answer: The lion capital (national emblem) on currency notes, coins, passports and government documents; the Ashoka Chakra on the national flag. A good message echoes dhamma — kindness, respect for everyone, non-violence, care for animals and nature.

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can explain how the Mauryan empire rose and how it was governed, including Ashoka’s dhamma
prompt: Predict: if Ashoka's messages had been written on wood or cloth instead of stone, what would we know about him today?
prompt_hi: Socho: agar Ashoka ke sandesh patthar ki jagah lakdi ya kapde par likhe hote, toh aaj hum unke baare mein kya jaante?
answer: Very little from his own words — wood and cloth rot away; much of our knowledge of Ashoka comes from stone edicts that survived for over 2,000 years (and were read again after James Prinsep deciphered Brahmi in the 1830s).

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can explain how the Mauryan empire rose and how it was governed, including Ashoka’s dhamma
prompt: Teach a younger cousin how Magadha became the Mauryan empire and how Ashoka ruled it. Use at least four steps.
prompt_hi: Chhote cousin ko samjhao ki Magadha kaise Maurya samrajya bana aur Ashoka ne ise kaise chalaya. Kam se kam chaar steps mein.
answer: Key idea: Magadha's resources made it strong; Chandragupta with Chanakya founded the Mauryan empire (c. 321 BCE); it was run through provinces, officials, army and spies; Ashoka fought the Kalinga war, regretted it, and ruled through dhamma, spreading it with edicts.

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can explain how the Mauryan empire rose and how it was governed, including Ashoka’s dhamma
prompt: An edict says everyone in Ashoka's empire was happy and well cared for. How should a historian treat this claim?
prompt_hi: Ek shilalekh kehta hai ki Ashoka ke samrajya mein sab khush the aur sabka dhyaan rakha jaata tha. Itihaaskar ko is daave ko kaise dekhna chahiye?
answer: As the ruler's own view and goals — useful evidence of what Ashoka wanted and believed — but it must be checked against other sources (archaeology, other texts, foreign accounts) before accepting it as what really happened.

subject: sst

answer: Around 185 BCE; the Shunga dynasty.

subject: sst

prompt_hi: Is samay ke map ko dekh ke shabdon mein batao ki kaun kahan raaj karta tha: Satavahana, Kushana, Chola-Chera-Pandya, aur Kharavela.
answer: Satavahanas: the Deccan (today's Maharashtra, Telangana, Andhra region). Kushanas: the north-west and north, from Central Asia and Afghanistan into the Ganga plains (Mathura). Cholas, Cheras and Pandyas: the far south (Tamil Nadu and Kerala). Kharavela: Kalinga (today's Odisha).

subject: sst

prompt_hi: Ek bada samrajya (Maurya jaisa) aur kai kshetriya rajya (unke baad jaise) compare karo: har ek ka ek fayda aur ek mushkil.
answer: Big empire: one set of rules and roads over a huge area (advantage) but hard to control far regions (challenge). Regional kingdoms: rulers close to local people, local languages and art grew (advantage) but more rivalry and wars between kingdoms (challenge).

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can describe the kingdoms that followed the Mauryas and the growth of trade and culture
prompt: Why did Roman traders want to trade with south India?
prompt_hi: Roman vyapaari dakshin Bharat se vyapar kyun karna chahte the?
answer: South India had goods Romans prized — especially black pepper, along with other spices, fine cotton cloth, pearls and gems — and Romans paid in gold and silver coins, wine and other goods.

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can describe the kingdoms that followed the Mauryas and the growth of trade and culture
prompt: Sailors learned to use the seasonal monsoon winds to cross the Arabian Sea directly. Predict what sea trade would have been like without these winds.
prompt_hi: Naavikon ne seekha ki mausami monsoon hawaon ka use karke Arabian Sea seedha paar kiya ja sakta hai. Socho: in hawaon ke bina samudri vyapar kaisa hota?
answer: Slower, riskier and costlier: ships would have to hug the coast, take longer routes and make fewer trips, so less trade would reach India and Rome.

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can describe the kingdoms that followed the Mauryas and the growth of trade and culture
prompt: Why was the Satavahana king called "Gautamiputra" Satakarni? What does this tell us?
prompt_hi: Satavahana raja ko "Gautamiputra" Satakarni kyun kaha jaata tha? Isse kya pata chalta hai?
answer: "Gautamiputra" means "son of Gautami" — Satavahana kings were often known by their mother's name, which shows that mothers held an important place in how royal identity was shown.

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can describe the kingdoms that followed the Mauryas and the growth of trade and culture
prompt: A Kushana gold coin shows a king in Central Asian dress on one side and the Buddha on the other. List three things a historian can learn from it.
prompt_hi: Ek Kushana sone ke sikke par ek taraf Madhya Asiya ke kapdon mein raja hai aur doosri taraf Buddha. Itihaaskar ise dekh ke teen kya baatein jaan sakta hai?
answer: Who the ruler was and how he wanted to be seen; that the Kushanas had Central Asian roots; that they respected or supported Buddhism; that the kingdom was rich and traded widely (it could mint gold coins).

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can describe the kingdoms that followed the Mauryas and the growth of trade and culture
prompt: Find the mistake: "Roman coins found in south India prove that the Romans ruled south India."
prompt_hi: Galti pakdo: "Dakshin Bharat mein mile Roman sikke saabit karte hain ki Romans ne dakshin Bharat par raaj kiya."
answer: Finding foreign coins shows trade, not rule: Roman traders paid with them for Indian goods. There is no evidence that Rome ruled south India.

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can describe the kingdoms that followed the Mauryas and the growth of trade and culture
prompt: Compare Buddha images in the Gandhara style and the Mathura style.
prompt_hi: Gandhara shaili aur Mathura shaili ki Buddha moortiyon ki tulna karo.
answer: Gandhara (north-west): influenced by Greek and Roman art — wavy hair, heavy folded robes, realistic face, often grey stone. Mathura: local style — reddish sandstone, rounder fuller figure, smiling face, thin clinging robe. Both show the Buddha but in different local styles.

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can describe the kingdoms that followed the Mauryas and the growth of trade and culture
prompt: What are the Sangam texts, and what do they tell us?
prompt_hi: Sangam granth kya hain, aur ve humein kya batate hain?
answer: Early Tamil poems composed over several centuries around this time; they describe life in the far south — kings (Cheras, Cholas, Pandyas), landscapes, love, war, trade and ports.

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can describe the kingdoms that followed the Mauryas and the growth of trade and culture
prompt: Think of something in your home that came from far away. How does it reach your town today, compared with how pepper reached Rome 2,000 years ago? What travels along with goods besides the goods themselves?
prompt_hi: Ghar mein koi cheez socho jo door se aayi ho. Aaj woh tumhare shehar tak kaise pahunchti hai, aur 2,000 saal pehle kaali mirch Rome tak kaise pahunchti thi? Saamaan ke saath aur kya-kya safar karta hai?
answer: Today: trucks, trains, container ships, planes, online orders; then: carts, pack animals, sailing ships using monsoon winds. Along with goods travel people, languages, ideas, food habits, art and religions.

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can describe the kingdoms that followed the Mauryas and the growth of trade and culture
prompt: Teach a friend why historians call this period an "age of reorganisation" and not an age of decline. Give three pieces of evidence.
prompt_hi: Dost ko samjhao ki itihaaskar is daur ko "punargathan ka yug" kyun kehte hain, patan ka nahi. Teen saboot do.
answer: Key idea: power was reorganised among many regional kingdoms, each with achievements. Evidence: growth of trade with Rome and Central Asia (Roman coins, ports); new coins (Indo-Greek portraits, Kushana gold, Satavahana coins); art and literature (Gandhara and Mathura art, Sangam poems); spread of Buddhism along trade routes.

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can describe the kingdoms that followed the Mauryas and the growth of trade and culture
prompt: Why did Buddhism spread to Central Asia and China during this period?
prompt_hi: Is samay Buddh dharm Madhya Asiya aur China tak kyun faila?
answer: Monks travelled with merchants along the busy trade routes, and rulers like the Kushana king Kanishka supported Buddhism; monasteries along the routes became resting places for traders and teachers.

answer: It tells us which rulers and regions Samudragupta fought or made submit, and how he wanted to be remembered. But it is a prashasti (praise poem) by his own court poet, so it is one-sided and may exaggerate; we check it against coins and other sources.

answer: The Aryabhatiya (499 CE). Ideas: the Earth spins on its axis (causing day and night); eclipses are caused by shadows; a very accurate value of pi (about 3.1416); use of the place-value system.

topic: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity

answer: The Earth itself spins on its axis, so the sky appears to move — like trees seeming to run backwards when you sit in a moving train.

subject: sst

topic: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity

answer: Wrong: a lunar eclipse happens when the Earth comes between the sun and the moon and its shadow falls on the moon; Aryabhata explained eclipses using shadows.

subject: sst

topic: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity

answer: Although it is made of iron and has stood in the open for about 1,600 years, it has hardly rusted; it shows the advanced metal-working skill of the time, and scientists study how its special composition and protective layer resist rust.

answer: Mauryas: edicts mostly in Prakrit (Brahmi script); remembered for a huge empire and Ashoka's dhamma. Guptas: courtly works mostly in Sanskrit; remembered for science, mathematics, literature, art and temples.

subject: sst
chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
topic: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
outcomes: Learner can describe achievements of the Gupta period in science, mathematics, art and literature

prompt_hi: Gupta kaal mein itni rachnaatmakta kyun hui? Teen kaaran batao.
answer: Kings and rich patrons supported scholars, poets and artists; wealth from farming and trade paid for buildings, art and learning; relative peace in the core regions; centres of learning like Nalanda where scholars could study and teach.

subject: sst
chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
topic: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
outcomes: Learner can describe achievements of the Gupta period in science, mathematics, art and literature
prompt: Was the Gupta period a "golden age" for everyone? Compare how a court poet and a farmer might have described their lives.
prompt_hi: Kya Gupta kaal sabke liye "swarn yug" tha? Ek darbaari kavi aur ek kisaan apni zindagi ka varnan kaise karte — tulna karo.
answer: A court poet, supported by the king, might describe wealth, beauty and learning. A farmer might describe hard work, taxes and dependence on rain. Most surviving sources come from courts and elites, so "golden age" fits some groups better than others; historians weigh both views.

subject: sst
chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
topic: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
outcomes: Learner can describe achievements of the Gupta period in science, mathematics, art and literature
prompt: A timeline shows: c. 320 CE Chandragupta I; c. 335 CE Samudragupta; c. 400 CE Faxian visits; 499 CE the Aryabhatiya is written. Tell this story in two sentences, in order, and say roughly how many years pass from the first mark to the last.
prompt_hi: Ek timeline par hai: lagbhag 320 CE Chandragupta I; lagbhag 335 CE Samudragupta; lagbhag 400 CE Faxian aate hain; 499 CE Aryabhatiya likhi jaati hai. Yeh kahaani do vaakyon mein kram se batao, aur pehle se aakhri nishaan tak lagbhag kitne saal hue?
answer: Chandragupta I began the Guptas' rise around 320 CE, and his son Samudragupta expanded the kingdom from about 335 CE. Around 400 CE the Chinese traveller Faxian visited, and in 499 CE Aryabhata wrote the Aryabhatiya — about 180 years after the first mark.

subject: sst
chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
topic: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity

prompt_hi: India ka pehla satellite, jo 1975 mein chhoda gaya, uska naam Aryabhata rakha gaya. Vaigyanikon ne yeh naam kyun chuna hoga? Apne din mein tum place-value wali sankhya pranaali kahan use karte ho?
answer: To honour an Indian pioneer of astronomy and mathematics. Place value is used everywhere: prices, phone numbers, cricket scores, page numbers, money (in 305, the 3 means 3 hundreds and the 0 holds the tens place).

subject: sst
chapter: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
topic: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity

prompt_hi: Socho: agar raja aur ameer sanrakshak kaviyon, vidvaanon aur kalakaaron ki madad karna band kar dete, toh Gupta kaal ki rachnaatmakta ka kya hota?
answer: Much less would have been created: scholars and artists need time, materials and a living to write books, paint caves or build temples; without patronage many would have had to do other work, so fewer works of science, art and literature would have been made or preserved.

subject: sst

answer: Key idea: science — Aryabhata (Earth's rotation, eclipses, pi) or the rust-resistant iron pillar; art — early stone temples (e.g. Deogarh) or the Ajanta cave paintings of the same period (made under the Vakatakas, Gupta allies); literature — Kalidasa's Shakuntalam or Meghaduta; caution — sources mainly show courts and elites, so it was not golden for everyone.

subject: sst

answer: Rivers (and their confluences), mountains, forests/groves (also lakes, springs, caves, certain trees).

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can explain how rivers, mountains, groves and pilgrimage routes became sacred and connected people across India
prompt: Why might a sangam — a place where rivers meet — be seen as especially sacred?
prompt_hi: Sangam — jahan nadiyaan milti hain — ko khaas taur par pavitra kyun maana ja sakta hai?
answer: Rivers give water, food and life; where two or more meet, the meeting of life-giving waters feels powerful and special, and such places became natural gathering points for people, rituals and fairs (like the Kumbh at Prayagraj).

subject: sst

prompt: The Char Dham are at four corners of India. Name each and say in which direction and state it lies. What does visiting all four suggest?
prompt_hi: Char Dham Bharat ke chaar konon par hain. Har ek ka naam, disha aur rajya batao. Chaaron ki yatra karna kya dikhata hai?
answer: Badrinath – north (Uttarakhand); Dwarka – west (Gujarat); Puri – east (Odisha); Rameswaram – south (Tamil Nadu). Visiting all four means crossing the whole land, which expresses the idea that the whole of India is one connected sacred land.

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can explain how rivers, mountains, groves and pilgrimage routes became sacred and connected people across India
prompt: Name the four places where the Kumbh Mela is held, with the river at each.
prompt_hi: Kumbh Mela jin chaar jagahon par lagta hai unke naam aur wahan ki nadi batao.
answer: Prayagraj (confluence of the Ganga and Yamuna, with the Saraswati of tradition), Haridwar (Ganga), Ujjain (Shipra), Nashik (Godavari).

subject: sst

prompt: Match each place with the tradition for which it is most famous: Bodh Gaya, Shravanabelagola, Golden Temple (Amritsar), Ajmer Sharif, Velankanni.

answer: Bodh Gaya – Buddhist (Buddha's enlightenment); Shravanabelagola – Jain (Gommateshwara statue); Golden Temple – Sikh; Ajmer Sharif – Sufi shrine (dargah of Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti), visited by people of many faiths; Velankanni – Christian (basilica in Tamil Nadu).

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can explain how rivers, mountains, groves and pilgrimage routes became sacred and connected people across India
prompt: How did pilgrimage connect different parts of India long ago?
prompt_hi: Puraane samay mein teerth yatra ne Bharat ke alag-alag hisson ko kaise joda?
answer: Pilgrims travelled long distances, met people of other regions, shared stories, songs, languages and food, and traders and artisans followed the routes; this created links and a shared sense of belonging across the land.

subject: sst
outcomes: Learner can explain how rivers, mountains, groves and pilgrimage routes became sacred and connected people across India
prompt: Predict: if all long pilgrimage routes had closed for a hundred years, what might have happened to the links between regions?
prompt_hi: Socho: agar saare lambe teerth raaste sau saal ke liye band ho jaate, toh kshetron ke beech ke rishton ka kya hota?
answer: Fewer people would travel between regions, so there would be less sharing of languages, stories, crafts, food and trade, and regions might feel more separate from each other.

subject: sst
